subsubtopic: ASSISTANCE SOUGHT FOR DAVIE SHIPBUILDING LTD. IN QUEBEC
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the situation at Davie Shipbuilding in Lauzon is a very difficult one at the present time. This major employer in the Quebec City region, ranking second behind the Quebec Civil Service, may be facing a very serious situation by the end of 1984, when construction on the CN Marine ferry will be terminated, because the shipyard does not seem to have any new projects on its order books.
When the contract for the frigates was awarded on June 29 of this year, the plan was that as a compensatory measure, Davie would be asked to proceed with refitting of the Tribal destroyers, for a project that was then estimated at $650 million.
I therefore urge the Government to proceed as soon as possible with the studies and preparations required to carry out this major contract. I also urge the Government of Quebec to show some favouritism towards Davie Shipyards and to stop playing games. It is a fact that P.Q. politicians in the Quebec City area have criticized the federal Government's measures with respect to Davie Shipyards, while they are not as eager to admit that the Government of Quebec, which, through the Societe generate de financement, owns Marine Industries Ltd. in Sorel, is supporting this shipyard on the outskirts of Montreal.
Finally, Madam Speaker, I urge the owners, the unions, the federal Government and the Government of Quebec to take action to save Davie Shipyards.

Madam Speaker, now hear this! Senator Michael Pitfield has opened "Pandora's Liberal Box" and told the nation the secret he held so closely with the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) for 25 years-the Liberals have been "throwing money" at their problems.
Thousands of Canadians have wondered why our deficit was increasing year by year. The Liberals have been throwing money at every problem that confronted them. With their own money? Of course not; with the people's money. Listen to what Senator Pitfield said in Toronto the other day, and I quote:
We have been solving governmental problems by throwing money at them.
The Liberals have been buying their way into office. When a Liberal MP became a problem, the Prime Minister and Michael Pitfield "threw money" at him and sent him on a trip with all expenses paid.
Was there a problem with the Prime Minister's secretary in his office? The Prime Minister and Michael Pitfield "threw money" at her and she studied French for a year at public expense in the Riveria.
Did Senator Pitfield himself become a problem to the Prime Minister? I guess so, because the Prime Minister "threw money" at him and sent him to the Senate with a pension for life.
Millions of people exist on UIC and welfare. Businesses have been forced into bankruptcy through National Energy Program taxes. No matter, the Liberals had to get the money somewhere to "throw money" at their problems. What a pity!

subsubtopic: FIFTIETH ANNIVERSARY OF SOVIET INDUCED FAMINE
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, this weekend marks the fiftieth anniversary of the great famine in the Soviet Ukraine. The forced famine, as it was known, resulted in between six million and ten million Ukranian peasants dying of starvation, starvation brought about by the inhuman policies of Joseph Stalin's regime. In spite of many offerings of assistance, the aid was rejected. Malcolm Mug-geridge, who was there at the time, wrote the following:
-the fields are covered with weeds and the people, swollen from hunger, are awaiting inevitable death. In talking to these miserable people you will find out how many have died from hunger and how many were executed by the Soviet

October 21, 1983
government or deported because they have hidden a little wheat in order to satisfy their hunger.
In the name of humanity we remember the victims, and vow that an ongoing vigilance will never allow this to recur in a world which is undoubtedly a world of some considerable danger.

subsubtopic: RESTRUCTURING OF PECHEURS-UNIS DU QUEBEC- ADVANTAGES TO PROVINCE OF PARTNERSHIP IN NEW CORPORATION
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the fishing industry plays a major part in the economy of the Gaspe peninsula, since 55 per cent of fish landings are made up of catches by fishermen in the riding of Gaspe and most fish processing plants are also in that riding. The Minister of Fisheries and Oceans (Mr. De Bane) has submitted a restructuration plan for Pecheurs-Unis du Quebec, with the three following objectives: to ensure that Pecheurs-Unis du Quebec or its successor will continue to be economically viable; to develop a fair restructuration process, bearing in mind both the economic and social impact; to promote the development of Quebec's marine fisheries in co-operation with the Atlantic fisheries. The directors of Pecheurs-Unis have agreed with the plan to set up a new company to administer the fishing industry in Quebec. Members of fishermen's co-operatives in Riviere-au-Renard, Newport and Saint-Maurice de I'Echouerie have expressed their agreement with the decision to accept the offer made by the Government of Canada, and the co-operative in Cloridorme will be doing so within a few hours.
On behalf of Quebec fishermen and processing plant workers, I urge the Government of Quebec to co-operate with the Government of Canada, in order to save Quebec's fishing industry from disaster, by setting up a new company administered by the people concerned and the financial institutions.

subtopic: CALL FOR REINSTATEMENT OF ATLANTIC LIMITED TRAIN
CALL FOR REINSTATEMENT OF ATLANTIC LIMITED TRAIN
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, passenger rail service in Atlantic Canada has been less than satisfactory since two well-utilized lines were abruptly abandoned 23 months ago. Since then neither New Brunswickers nor other Maritimers have experienced the improved, cost-efficient service, or seen the new equipment the former Minister of Transport, the current Minister of State for External Relations (Mr. Pepin), advised us the sacrifices were being made for at that time.
[DOT] (mo)
Instead, many communities are left without public transportation, schedules are chaotic, trains are overbooked, obliging passengers to stand cheek-to-cheek and cheek-to-cheek, and the LRCs, promised to be in operation by the summer of 1983, proved to be another promise shattered.
1 urge the Minister to use every resource available to him to reinstate the popular, time and economically efficient and respected Atlantic Limited in an effort to reverse the tawdry and disgraceful service New Brunswickers have endured for the past two years. Forcing passengers to travel backwards before travelling forward, at greater expense and less convenience, does not forge a dynamic rail service.
The decision to terminate one of Canada's most popular lines is indicative of the irresponsibility of the Government in making this decision, and shows a general lack of compassion for and appreciation of the basic needs of Atlantic Canadians. Sadly, it is compatible with many other of its decisions adversely affecting the region.

subtopic: EXPENDITURES ON OFFICIAL RESIDENCE OF LEADER OF THE OPPOSITION
EXPENDITURES ON OFFICIAL RESIDENCE OF LEADER OF THE OPPOSITION
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise today to speak on the same topic as the Hon. Member for Bow River (Mr. Taylor). Canadians are tired of the ever-growing examples of how Government officials have been both negligent and extravagant when it comes to spending somebody else's money.
In the case of Stornoway, the rent-free accommodation of the Leader of the Official Opposition, in the last seven years the residents of that house spent $25,000 in 1976, $25,000 in 1979, $35,000 in 1980, and the latest tenant, the new Leader of the Conservative Party (Mr. Mulroney), has found it necessary to spend $50,000 of taxpayers' dollars on a splash or two of paint.
This latest example of living high at the public trough raises a number of questions. First, to justify the expenditure of $50,000, did the Leader of the Conservative Party sign a long-term lease for Stornoway? Second, what political party does a leader belong to when he acts like a Liberal, lives like a Liberal, and spends other people's money like a Liberal?
Finally, with the Prime Minister's power as the custodian of the national treasury, can Canadians afford to move this free spender from Stornoway to 24 Sussex?

subtopic: COVERAGE OF DEBATE ON WESTERN GRAIN TRANSPORTATION
COVERAGE OF DEBATE ON WESTERN GRAIN TRANSPORTATION
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the House of Commons is gripped in the vise of an historical debate over changes to the Crow rate. That debate is of enormous economic and historical importance. This is an issue of deep-rooted differences, but one that impacts on industrial central Canada just as much as on western farmers. It is a major national issue, yet our national media have failed miserably at understanding and explaining the issue.
Last night CTV news won the award for gross incompetence. After a difficult day in the House of Commons in which the Crow rate legislation was the central issue, the news coverage was inadequate in time and content, and bland in delivery.
While our nation is struggling with an issue that contributes $6 billion annually to our balance of payments, more than any other single commodity, the issue tends to be viewed as a western one rather than as a national one, largely because the national media and central Canada are synonymous. We should not be surprised by this. The head office for CBC radio is in Ottawa; the head office for CBC TV is in Ottawa; the head office for Global TV is in Toronto; the head office for CTV is in Toronto; the head office for Maclean's magazine is
Oral Questions
in Toronto, and the head office for CP wire service is in Toronto. The media are in central Canada.
It is unfortunate and dangerous that our national media are centralized to the extent that they are incapable of understanding and explaining national issues whose origins are in the regions apart from central Canada. Unfortunately, the disadvantages must be shared by all Canadians.

Madam Speaker, my question is directed to the Acting Prime Minister. Would the Acting Prime Minister indicate if he was quoted correctly and, if so, if he was speaking for the Government when he was reported to have stated yesterday that the Canadian Government, after a reasonable, decent period of time, would likely recognize the new Government in Grenada? I ask this, Madam Speaker, in view of the fact that the Government of Jamaica, the Government of Barbados and the Governments of other Commonwealth Caribbean nations have already indicated that they do not intend to follow that course.

speakeroldname: Hon. Jean-Luc Pepin (Minister of State (External Relations)):
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I remember teaching this subject to my students 20 years ago. There are two approaches to the phenomenon of recognizing de facto governments. One is referred to as the objective approach and the other is referred to as the subjective approach. Generally speaking, Canada has taken the objective approach to recognition of government, that is, we of course wait over a period of time and try to find out answers to a number of questions.
We need to find out what the relations will be between the government in question and neighbouring governments, and what the reality of the administration exercised by that government will be. We have to look at the attitude of the government to its own citizens. After a decent period of time, which is to be qualified in each case, the phenomenon of objective recognition takes place. It is a rather complex issue. Such recognition took place just a few days ago in the case of one of the African governments.

Madam Speaker, my question is again directed to the Acting Prime Minister who, frankly, rather startles me with that type of a reply. Would the Acting Prime Minister indicate if he is aware of the fact that the National Mobilization Minister in Grenada, Selwyn Stra-chan, has stated that he believes there is room for comradely

October 21, 1983
Oral Questions
assistance to revolutions in the Caribbean? Mr. Strachan is presumably to be one of the new cabinet Ministers in Grenada. In that context, would the Minister at least indicate to the House whether he has consulted with the United Kingdom or with other Caribbean Commonwealth countries to determine what steps should now be taken, in view of the brutal and violent seizure of power in Grenada?

speakeroldname: Hon. Jean-Luc Pepin (Minister of State (External Relations)):
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I try to be a bit constructive when answering these questions. I was asked by the press yesterday about what would happen, and I did my very best to try to describe the phenomenon as it would take place. Indeed, we will consult with the Governments of different West Indies islands. There is a meeting of West Indian Commonwealth Governments during the coming weekend, I undestand. We will be listening to their views on the subject. However, I cannot but describe it the way it is, and I cannot but repeat what I have already said.
When a government, a group of people, a junta or whatever, takes over power in a country by force, we must look at all of the factors that I have indicated. Those factors include the reality of the exercise of power, and the reaction of the neighbouring countries to that exercise of power. A sort of consensus builds up in the world and, after a period of time, the facts of life are accepted and recognition is given. By using the standards that the Hon. Member seems to imply, he would probably have refused to recognize the previous Government of Grenada in any event.

Madam Speaker, again my question is directed to the Acting Prime Minister, and perhaps it could be answered better if I were more specific.
There has been some $10 million worth of Canadian aid going into Grenada. Various programs are now under way, including improvements for port facilities, the improvement of a central garage facility, and other aid projects. In view of the fact that in other countries when there is a serious question about the safety of our aid personnel, the aid programs are suspended, would the Minister indicate if that is now under consideration with respect to the continuing programs for Grenada?

speakeroldname: Hon. Jean-Luc Pepin (Minister of State (External Relations)):
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I think you have to start with the proposition that foreign aid, development aid, is not for the sake of recipient governments; it is for the sake of the people in the less developed countries. Consequently, we keep that in mind all the time-what is the interests of the people? In this particular instance $8.7 million has already been spent in the past in Grenada, and there is $1.6 million in current programs. With respect to the existing program, the purpose is to try to do as much as possible, which may not be much, because of the circumstances. The objective is to try to continue with the existing program.
With respect to future programs, obviously they are not in the making now. Again, it is reality that we try to cope with in this particular instance, and the interests of the people of Grenada.

Madam Speaker, my question is likewise addressed to the Minister who is Acting Prime Minister today but who, on Wednesday, was junior Minister of External Affairs. I wonder if he could tell the House whether the Prime Minister, who never fails to remind us of the great role he plays in the North-South dialogue, has had any discussion with the heads of the Caribbean Governments or with the President of the United States, on this brutal take-over in Grenada, with a view to concerting action, whether it be recognition, or other action in the hemisphere against the vicious Government now in place in Grenada?

speakeroldname: Hon. Jean-Luc Pepin (Minister of State (External Relations)):
speechtext: Madam Speaker, I have already referred to the forthcoming Commonwealth Caribbean countries' meeting. Obviously we will be in consultation with them on the result of their meeting during the weekend.

subtopic: COMMONWEALTH CARIBBEAN MEETING-REQUEST THAT CANADIAN OBSERVER ATTEND
COMMONWEALTH CARIBBEAN MEETING-REQUEST THAT CANADIAN OBSERVER ATTEND
speechtext: Madam Speaker, as was mentioned the other day, there are some 85 Canadians in Grenada at the present time, some as travellers and some as "cooperants" in the CIDA projects. I wonder if the Acting Prime Minister could tell the House whether any approach has been made to the Commonwealth Caribbean Ministers who are meeting today about whether Canada, as a member of the Commonwealth, could send an observer to that meeting so that we can know what actions are being concerted, and could fall in line with them?

speakeroldname: Hon. Jean-Luc Pepin (Minister of State (External Relations)):
subtopic: COMMONWEALTH CARIBBEAN MEETING-REQUEST THAT CANADIAN OBSERVER ATTEND
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, my hon. friend does not seem to realize how confused the situation is. There are three or four versions of what took place, so every government in the world, including the Canadian Government is simply trying to find out what is happening.
With respect to the Canadians there, the number has already been referred to, and the information we have is that they are in contact with each other. As you know, there is one diplomat from our High Commission in Barbados now in Grenada. They are in contact with each other, and the information of the Department of External Affairs is that, generally, they are in a reasonably good mood. They have been told not to move because there is a curfew, and it is considered by the Department that if they start getting out of their hotels and homes at this time they would be more in danger than if they stayed put. That is the advice that has been given to them.
October 21, 1983

Madam Speaker, the Acting Prime Minister will know that the Commonwealth Ministers are meeting today. They have all said they will not recognize that regime. Is the Acting Prime Minister suggesting that Canada is going to be out of step with the other Commonwealth members in this hemisphere, in recognizing that regime after a decent delay? After this atrocious occurrence in Grenada will Canada recognize that regime, after a decent delay?

speakeroldname: Hon. Jean-Luc Pepin (Minister of State (External Relations)):
speechtext: No, Madam Speaker, I specifically said the opposite. I mentioned that among the factors which are borne in mind in the process of deciding whether or not recognition of a government should be given, is the conduct of that de facto in its relationships with neighbouring countries. Of course, one way in which we come to our decision is by looking to and consulting with neighbouring countries on what they will do. If, for a number of reasons, all the neighbouring countries of Grenada should decide not to grant recognition for a period of time-for a long period of time-I am sure this would be a major consideration in the decision Canada would have to make.

subsubtopic: GOVERNMENT POSITION ON TESTING OF CRUISE MISSILES
speechtext: Madam Speaker, in the absence of the Prime Minister I would like to direct my question to the Acting Prime Minister. The Prime Minister himself is reported to have set up a task force concerned with ways to ease East-West tensions. And the Government is reported to be going to spend some $500,000 this coming year on a verification program having to do with the arms race. Can the Acting Prime Minister tell this House, and the many Canadians who will be expressing their support of nuclear disarmament this weekend, how the Government reconciles this concern for verification procedures, on the one hand, with the decision of the very same Government to test the Cruise missile, a missile whose most distinctive and most frightening feature is its very unverifiability?

subsubtopic: GOVERNMENT POSITION ON TESTING OF CRUISE MISSILES
speechtext: Just like the SS-20s.

speakeroldname: Hon. Jean-Luc Pepin (Minister of State (External Relations)):
subsubtopic: GOVERNMENT POSITION ON TESTING OF CRUISE MISSILES
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, in Canada we will find that easy to reconcile because we have decided, in conjunction with our NATO allies, to take a two-track approach-to defend ourselves properly and adequately and, at the same time, to do everything we can to bring about peace, disarmament, and so on. Those two things are easy to reconcile. I am sure that 99 per cent of the people of Canada have already reconciled them.
Oral Questions
With respect to the task force, indeed there is such a task force, and one would be expected to have such a task force. At the Williamsburg Summit the leaders pledged themselves, and promised they would do everything-and more colourful words were used at that time-to bring about peace and, particularly, to bring about forms of disarmament. Therefore, the task force is really in line with that pledge. The Prime Minister is collecting views from our own diplomats around the world as to what, when, where and how could East-West tensions be reduced. That is the purpose of the task force, and the Prime Minister, when he is at Guelph in a few days, will have a chance to give us his thinking on that particular subject.

subsubtopic: GOVERNMENT POSITION ON TESTING OF CRUISE MISSILES
speechtext: Madam Speaker, how often do we have to listen to the line that this is in keeping with our NATO commitments? Expert after expert has said that this has nothing to do with NATO. If the Government is concerned about NATO, there are other ways in which it could beef up its commitment to NATO.

subtopic: REQUEST THAT GOVERNMENT RECONSIDER MISSILE TESTING DECISION
REQUEST THAT GOVERNMENT RECONSIDER MISSILE TESTING DECISION
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, we hear the Acting Prime Minister, like the Prime Minister, putting a lot of faith in arms control talks, talks which many experts, including Elva Myrdal, the Nobel Peace Prize winner of last year, has said are worth nil as far as real nuclear disarmament is concerned. Is the Government now prepared to admit, on the eve of this weekend when we hope the Prime Minister will make a half decent speech in Guelph, that these talks are not enough, that they are no substitute for courageous action to break the hold of the nuclear whirlpool on this planet?
Will the Acting Prime Minister now, in the name of the Government, indicate a willingness on the part of the Government to reconsider the testing of the Cruise missile? And would he also indicate at the same time the Government's position on other proposals, such as the call for a freeze on the testing, deployment, and development of new nuclear weapons? This is called "suffociation" in case the Acting Prime Minister and the Prime Minister do not know what that word means.

speakeroldname: Hon. Jean-Luc Pepin (Minister of State (External Relations)):
subtopic: REQUEST THAT GOVERNMENT RECONSIDER MISSILE TESTING DECISION
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the Hon. Member was obviously more interested in preparing his second question than in listening to the answer I gave to his first question. I referred to the two-track approach. Most people who think about these problems, and many, many many do, are sort of reconciled with the fact that it makes sense that you try to protect yourself in the best possible way. That is a prudent decision to make. Yet at the same time you do your utmost to develop a spirit of co-operation in the field to bring about peace through disarmament. That is what the Secretary of State for External Affairs declared the other day.

October 21, 1983
Oral Questions
Canada has always been very conscious of the importance of verification as an ingredient of disarmament. What the Secretary of State declared the other day was not new, it was a continuation, with more money being assigned to it. But Canada is active, and the rest of the world thinks so, in all fora, employing all means or devices which can be used to bring about disarmament. We are active in the field of control of chemical weapons, outer space, and what not. So, to quote what was said at the time of the Williamsburg Conference, we really do our utmost to bring about better conditions for peace.

speechtext: Madam Speaker, when will the blind see, and when will this Government see, that there is no protection to be had in the kind of arms race towards which it is contributing as the Canadian Government?

speechtext:

Jet, owned by the federal Government, be sent to Europe to ferry him about the Middle East, and that the Jet was sent with empty seats while the Minister flew commercially? If that is so, what is the Minister's reason for doing that? Is it that he is uncertain about the airworthiness of the Challenger Jet, or is it, as the press reports, that the Challenger Jet would be forced to put down at Iceland to refuel and the Minister does not like the weather in Iceland this time of year?

speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subsubtopic: MINISTER'S USE OF CHALLENGER JET ON MIDDLE EAST TOUR
speechtext: It is too slow by boat.

speakeroldname: Hon. Jean-Luc Pepin (Minister of State (External Relations)):
subsubtopic: MINISTER'S USE OF CHALLENGER JET ON MIDDLE EAST TOUR
speechtext: Madam Speaker, the answer is, as usual, quite simple. It is to save time. The Secretary of State is rather a busy man. subsubtopic: WHITE FARM EQUIPMENT LTD.-BIDS FOR COMPANY
speechtext: Madam Speaker, I would like to address a question to the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce on behalf of grain producers who have millions of dollars invested in White Farm equipment, and on behalf of the 150 plus dealers of White Canada. In view of the fact that the receiver is meeting today to review bids for White Canada, could the Minister inform the House how many realistic, firm bids have been made for the White assets, and if any of those bidders are Canadian?

speakerposition: Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce; Minister of Regional Economic Expansion
subsubtopic: WHITE FARM EQUIPMENT LTD.-BIDS FOR COMPANY
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, this week for the first time since the process started the receiver has received three bona fide bids. I understand the creditors have recommended that the receiver proceed to the bankruptcy court with a recommendation for the Borg-Warner proposal. The Borg-Warner board is meeting today with respect to adopting the conditions the receiver has
Oral Questions
put forward on behalf of the creditors in determining the commercial terms. That this House condemns the Government for its failure to recognize the economic hardship affecting all farmers in Canada, and its failure to help alleviate that hardship by implementing sound agricultural policies.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: The Hon. Member for Portage-Marquette.
Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, 1 hope everyone will give me the same kind of reception after I finish speaking! This is certainly a great opportunity to talk about a very basic part of any country. If we are to be a sovereign country, we first have to assure an adequate food supply. When we speak to that, we speak to what goes on in Canadian agriculture.
In the past Canadian agriculture has served the country extremely well. It is the reason Canada was settled in the first place. There were vast amounts of land available. People came from literally all over the world to take advantage of the land and the opportunity to develop it and to plan for the future. Unfortunately, in the last 15 years or so this Government in particular has been extremely derelict in ensuring the same kind of opportunity for farmers now as was the case when the country was originally settled some 50 or 75 years ago, in the case of western Canada, or in many cases as many as 200 years ago and more in other parts of the country.
Agriculture is extremely important to any society. We can almost define any developed country in terms of the amount of disposable income its people have to spend to feed themselves. Recently figures were made available which showed that the average consumer in Canada spent something like 16 per cent of his or her disposable income or take-home pay on food. This means that there is 84 per cent left to do other things. Also it means that we can have shorter work weeks, holidays with pay and many of the amenities which have come to be taken for granted but are basically luxuries in other parts of the world. These are the types of things an efficient agricultural system provides and are necessary for a developed society.
Other parts of the world are unfortunately not as well off as we are. People spend as much as 50 per cent or 60 per cent of their income or time on feeding themselves. This means they do not have time for shorter work weeks and that basically they have to work long hours in the fields.
We are very fortunate. The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) has said many times-and I agree with him-that we have a very efficient system of agriculture. I would argue that it has become efficient in many cases despite government policy. This speaks to the ingenuity of individual farmers. That same ingenuity is what attracted people to settle the country in
the first place; that same ingenuity made agriculture more productive.
When I say "16 per cent", that only tells part of the story. The 16 per cent of disposable income spent on food also includes many meals eaten away from the home. They are increasing. In the neighbourhood of 30 per cent to 40 per cent of all meals consumed in Canada are prepared outside the home. In addition, they include various fruits and vegetables which are out of season. This means they have to be transported into the country, which speaks to our balance of payments. In many cases this involves prepackaged and prepared food. It has been said that a potato does not go into a modern kitchen unless it is peeled. In many cases that is true. That is the kind of thing we take for granted today, in many ways at the peril of agriculture.
In the last two or three decades farming has changed. In many ways farmers were previously looked at as second-class citizens. For example, if a person was a poor driver, he was a farmer; he did not know how to drive because he had never been in a city. Now farmers are very sophisticated. We cannot tell the city kids any longer from the country kids. We all wear the same kind of clothes. We work with computers. We are a very modern, productive, forward-looking and energetic group of people. Unfortunately, the present Government has not kept pace with what Canadian agriculture is doing.
This motion is a very broad one and it is easy to condemn people out of hand, but I would like to be more specific by talking about it in terms of money, the basic problem of most of the country today. Certainly agriculture is no different, but in many ways its situation is a unique one. One of the ways agriculture has become more productive is that it has mainly become more capital-intensive. It now takes as many dollars to create a job in Canadian agriculture as it does in Canadian manufacturing. Farmers now need money to farm. They also need seed, fertilizer and modern machinery. They need access to capital. Certainly that speaks to government policy. As we all know, Government has become a very large factor in anybody's life today. That is what is going on in Canadian agriculture.
Many things could be done in the area of agricultural finance which do not require the spending of a lot of money. I would like to refer to some of the questions I am asked for which I do not have answers because the Government does not have any policies directed at answering such questions. When farmers see that there are term deposits in banks in the neighbourhood of 6 per cent, 7 per cent or 8 per cent, when they see the Farm Credit Corporation offering money at over 13 per cent, and when they see chartered banks offering money at the same rate, they wonder why they cannot have access to funds at lower rates. This makes sense because it means Canadians would be given a chance to invest in the most basic industry in any modern society. This would not involve a lot of subsidy.
We saw the attitude of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) in Question Period today. The Government is giving things to people. It has given money to various sectors of
October 21, 1983

industry. Fanners are not asking to be given anything; they want to pay their own way. They want to be able to hold up their heads. This is what has made them very productive in the past. They are asking for an opportunity to pay their own way.
There are many things in the area of financing which could be done that would not require large Government expenditures. They are not big ticket items as far as Government moneys are concerned; in many ways they are just common sense. It makes no sense that we should raise fuel taxes. It is extremely expensive to fill a tractor before going to the field in the morning. If one fills up a 100-gallon fuel tank on a tractor-and there are many farm tractors with fuel tanks that size-as much as $ 100 in taxes goes into it. That is the kind of commitment a farmer has to meet when putting in spring crops. That money is not circulated back into the private sector, it goes to the Government. If we are having financial trouble, it does not make any sense to tax farmers to the brink of financial disaster on one hand, and on the other hand bring in programs that cost them money to assist them. That is a much simpler way of seeing that farmers stay in business and stay productive.
There are other things that could be done and some of my colleagues will outline them later in this debate. We are talking not only about western grain but the advance payments program. In many cases that has served us well. It puts money into the hands of the producers when they harvest their crops. If the crop is marketed over a period of time, it serves the Government and it serves the farm community very well.
In the case of the advance payments Act for western grain, it does not make sense that the Government does not increase the amount. Looking at the history of that program, it has served very well. The losses have been minimal. The Government pays the interest on it. The Canadian Wheat Board borrows the money at prime minus one-quarter per cent, which is better than any farmer can get. The more money that can be borrowed by the Canadian Wheat Board at prime minus one-quarter per cent to be put into circulation in the farm economy is better for the whole system, yet this Government refuses to increase cash advances to western farmers.
1 have had an opportunity to question the Minister on the agri-bond concept. It is still a concept, something that can be worked out. It is designed to allow the money generated in agriculture to stay in agriculture. It makes no sense, when a farmer sells out and wants to use that money as his retirement plan, to put it into the economy through trust funds, term deposits and so on in order to minimize the tax that he will have to pay on that money. What is wrong about developing incentives to have that money which was generated in agriculture remain in agriculture? It would alleviate some of the requirements for funds of the FCC and alleviate some of the requirements of the Minister of Agriculture on the banking institutions. However, we see no innovative proposals in terms of finance coming from this Government or this Minister.
Supply
A year ago last June 1 heard the Minister of Agriculture state over the radio that very shortly the Farm Credit Corporation would have a billion dollars available to loan to farmers at preferred rates of interest. However, we find that the FCC cannot even go to the domestic market to raise funds. That makes absolutely no sense. It further propagates the Minister's reputation as being somebody who likes to talk a lot and do very little. That is very unfortunate for the farmers of this country.
In many ways there is excessive regulation of the farming industry in this country. There is concern in western Canada about what is going on with producer cars. There are not enough available. That is one way the farmers can market their grain and save handling costs. There are problems in the British Columbia orchard industry. I am told that if the producers gave their product to the canneries, the canneries could not be competitive in their marketing with the products coming from offshore. There are problems on the east coast with the potato industry.
This Government has failed to negotiate on a square basis with the Americans. The Americans are our best neighbour and best trading partner. That does not mean that we have to roll over and play dead when it comes to negotiating with them. This Government has not maintained the proper connections with the Americans with whom we want to trade. They have to trade with us. They send us a lot of fruit and vegetables when they are not in season in Canada, as well as those we cannot produce. We certainly hold an ace as far as our trade with the United States is concerned. The Minister has not used that to the best advantage of our producers.
Let me touch briefly on what I believe is the real tragedy, and that is the attitude that seems to pervade the present Government. Agriculture is not asking for handouts, only an opportunity to be productive. Agriculture does not need a lot of subsidies and concessions, only a chance to be productive. If we can be competitive in world markets, we do not need a lot of the assistance and support that comes from time to time. What is needed is a proper economic climate.
The tragedy of this Government's agriculture policy is that it staggers from pillar to post. It reacts to situations once they are in place rather than looking at research and development. Some very exciting things are happening in research and development. There is the possibility of developing legume cereals which would very much reduce the cost of production and assist our producers in being competitive. What does this Government do? It cuts back on the amount of basic research. Our research is down the line once the product has been produced. Our producers should be armed with the best varieties and the best research in terms of pesticides, insecticides, fertilizer and so on. They would then be more than competitive.
This Government has failed to maintain a good climate for negotiations with the Provinces. We see a good example of that now in the stabilization program for red meats. I understand the federal Government took no meaningful part in the discussions and that is a tragedy. We had a debate in this

October 21, 1983
Supply
House a couple of years ago when we talked about the Constitution and all kinds of other things which the federal Government needed in order to have some clout. There is much that could be done with a simple change of attitude.
It would have been a lot more helpful to the livestock industry if the federal Government had participated fully in that program. It should have been at the table encouraging the negotiations and the development of a program. It could have said how much money it was willing to put on the table. It knows from the past that all the Provinces got into the act simply because the federal Government refused to get into the stabilizaton field as far as red meats are concerned.
The Minister has been derelict and negligent in this area. Because of that the four Provinces which represent 80 per cent of cattle production in this country have had to sit down together. The four Provinces recently reached an agreement in principle on how to proceed on the basis of a three-party program involving the Provinces, producers and the federal Government. We still do not know whether the federal Government will get involved and, if so, how much money it will put up. It is my information that all the federal Government contingency plans have been made on the basis that the Provinces would not arrive at an agreement. That is ridiculous as far as the federal Government and Minister are concerned. They are not in a position at the meetings to negotiate or show any leadership. They will not say how much money they will put on the table to see that this comes about.
I also recommend that the Agricultural Stabilization Act be used. In British Columbia there is a stabilization payment that has been due since 1982. It is not yet made. The Agricultural Stabilization Act needs to be overhauled in terms of the time period. It was moved from ten years to five years, and you can make the argument that it should be moved to a three-year average. The point is that whatever program is used, surely it should be incumbent upon the Government and the present Minister to see that it is administered in such a way that the payments are made at a time when they mean something. Producers in British Columbia have managed to survive for a whole year without payments being made. That calls into question the seriousness with which the Minister takes his responsibility.
I have almost run out of time and 1 would like to conclude, if 1 may, by making two or three suggestions that will not solve all of the problems but will at least show the producers that the Government is at least aware of the serious situation that exists with agriculture and recognizes how important agriculture is to a country like Canada. I have not mentioned how important agriculture is in terms of the balance of payments and that agricultural exports amount to some $9 billion. I have not mentioned the problems that the Minister seems to be ignoring in many of the other segments of agriculture, like the sheep industry or the Western Grain Stabilization Act. I have not mentioned any of those things. If I could take another 20
minutes, Mr. Speaker, I could outline the areas of responsibility that the Government and the Minister have not addressed.
Let me first suggest that the Minister take seriously the Agricultural Stabilization Act and that he see that there are enough people in his Department to administer it properly so that the payments are made on time and as quickly as possible after a crop has been harvested and the information is available as to whether or not there should be a payout. That is the very least the Minister can do. That would affect agricultural producers right across the country.
Let me also suggest to the Minister that he should move as quickly as he can to increase the level of cash advances. That is something that has been called for by all segments of the industry. It is something that would cost the Government a very, very minimal amount of money because, as I have already said, the history of that program in the past has shown that the losses have been minimal. When the Government does pick up the interest costs, as everyone appreciates, the interest costs are based on borrowing money at prime rate minus one-quarter of a per cent.
These are actions that are not earth shattering, but to take these actions would at least show the agriculture industry that the Government and the Minister have some interest in agriculture and are interested in seeing that efficiency continues to be improved and that the Canadian public continues to be served. The main thing is that agriculture continue to provide opportunities for young farmers to have the jobs that are so desperately needed.

Mr. Speaker, I note that the Hon. Member for Portage-Marquette (Mr. Mayer) spent a good part of his time outlining three topics. Two of those topics were more cash advances and easier credit which, while I refer to them as two different topics, are probably addressing the same problem of lack of cash. The third topic was the stabilization programs and I would focus my question on that topic for the moment.
The Hon. Member seems to think that the current base for the stabilization programs that now exist is fine and that the only real shortcoming is that too many years are thrown into the average. He has suggested that we move from the current five years to a three-year period. Does the Hon. Member not think that there is something inherently wrong with the base of the historical market price which those five or ten or three years give to the formula? Would he not think that we would be better off with a system that is based on costs rather than on market price, that would follow the actual costs from year to year and provide a much better form of stability to producers? Why did he ignore the possibility of moving to a cost base rather than simply trying to extend and make the old historically based data work?

Mr. Speaker, I certainly did not say that at all. If the Hon. Member wants to deal with the whole question of stabilization, it would take a long time because it is a very, very involved topic. All I suggested was that the Government at least be serious about the programs it has in place and administer them the way they were legislated.
October 21, 1983

There are many, many areas in the whole concept of stabilization that can be looked at and changed to improve the situation. In the meantime, the only thing we should ask the Government to do is to have the courtesy, the decency and the guts to administer properly what it already has in place so that at least we would know there is someone here doing something to take an interest in the farming community in the country.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to address a question to the Hon. Member because I did not hear part of his speech very well. I know the Hon. Member for Portage-Marquette (Mr. Mayer) touched upon the subject of financing but I did not hear him express whether or not he in fact knew that the Farm Credit Corporation was so low on funds that in some areas only 20 per cent of the people are being served by the Farm Credit Corporation and that 1,000 farmers are now stuck with an interest rate of 16% per cent. Of those 1,000 farmers, one-third are under the subsidization program and have had their interest rates lowered by 4 per cent. They will face an interest rate of 16% per cent again in the coming year. Even now they are not able to afford a rate of 12% per cent. I did not hear the Hon. Member mention that and I wondered if he could comment on that.

Mr. Speaker, that is a very, very sad situation which is occurring among a lot of farmers in the country. In many ways, those farmers were forced into the 16% per cent interest rate in the first place because it was either accept that kind of an interest rate or simply not be able to survive for another year. Certainly the attitude of the present Minister is that what he says and what he does are two entirely different things. He has gone on record as saying that he does not want to see the Farm Credit Corporation become a lender of last resort. I will agree with him. Yet the actions of the Government force the Farm Credit Corporation into becoming a lender of last resort so it is not able to address the problems that the Hon. member for Bruce-Grey (Mr. Gurbin) mentioned.
Certainly there should be room in the new Farm Credit Corporation Act, Bill C-88, that we in the House passed some 18 months ago to provide specifically for the Farm Credit Corporation to have authorization, with the concurrence of the Minister of Finance, to raise funds by any means it sees fit. These means would include some of the agri-bond concepts or access to domestic markets if the Minister of Agriculture could convince the Minister of Finance to let the Farm Credit Corporation go ahead with that. If some of those things could be done, then the Farm Credit Corporation would be in a position to borrow funds at a cheaper interest rate and look after some of the problems that it will have once these farmers are again forced to pay an interest rate of 16% per cent.

Mr. Speaker, I have another question for the Hon. Member for Portage-Marquette. When discussing the situation of the Farm Credit Corporation and the financing that is available through it, does the Hon. Member know of any specific proposal brought forward by the Government or discussed privately that would in fact indicate that the Minis-
Supply
ter of Agriculture has done anything at all in the past four years since he has again become Minister of Agriculture to help the long-term financing situation in agriculture?
Mr. Speaker, I guess it is with a great deal of sadness and a lot of lament that I must simply answer no.

speakeroldname: Hon. E. F. Whelan (Minister of Agriculture):
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member who is the agriculture critic for the Official Opposition has spoken and I am sure the record will show how good the first part of his speech was. He talked about efficiency in the agriculture industry and how it had developed over a period of years. He then tried to say that things had changed in the last 10 or 15 years. Things have changed. We are very proud of the vast majority of those changes because they have been for the better. There never have been such advances in agriculture as have taken place since November, 1972 when I was appointed Minister of Agriculture. These advances are the envy of the world. The huge superpowers that send people into space, send others to this country to see how we farm. For instance, 55 per cent of our farming takes place further north than in any other nation. People cannot understand how we do what we do, thanks to the Department of Agriculture and our research.
Oh, oh!

I can tell the Hon. Member from away down on the East Coast that even in his Province where agriculture is successful, it is because of the Department of Agriculture and its research. Research was established in Canada practically when agriculture started. We had experimental farms in western Canada before we had provinces. When settlers first moved into that area they realized the importance of having information available. Other nations that have been settled for 300 years are doing what we did at the beginning. Some say that research should be isolated and not mobile. The main research station is located in this city at the present time, although it was not in the city when it was first established over 100 years ago; but now it is in the centre of the capital of Canada, and is our largest research station.
Marquis wheat was developed in eastern Canada at our Ottawa station, and it has made Canada a power in the production of wheat. Some people said that that area of western Canada would never be farmed. Marquis wheat has made us a super food power through the research developed at the station in this city.
We have recently developed a new variety of wheat. The researchers told me to wait for another couple of years and they would put out a new variety called Columbus for the far northern regions. It has a husk that will allow the grain to withstand excessive moisture and other conditions. In two years it can mean up to a 4 per cent increase in wheat production in western Canada. That one variety of wheat took 14 years for researchers to develop. And there is a new program for a new variety of Columbus that will even be superior to the original.

October 21, 1983
Supply
It is for these reasons that other countries send people to visit our research stations and exchange scientists with us. We have readily signed such agreements with other countries, because no matter what we do by ourselves, if it is in isolation we can never feed the world. In 1980, the population of the world was 4.2 billion people. By the year 2000 it will be nearly six billion and in 20 years we will see the largest increase in population ever in history. The greatest challenge of all, therefore, is to produce food and to assist people in producing it.
Some Members have mentioned travelling. Perhaps they should see the travel vouchers I sign for our officials to go all over the world in order to assist other people in the control of disease and better plant production. My budget from the federal Government is not great, only 1.4 per cent of total federal expenditures, but a good portion of it goes for assistance to other countries. We have one of the healthiest agricultural industries in the world.
The Hon. Member's motion mentions "all farmers" but, Mr. Speaker, 50 per cent of farmers in Canada have no debts whatsoever; 35 per cent have still about an 85 per cent equity in their holdings, so only between 5 per cent and 15 per cent of our farmers are in some kind of financial difficulty.
It has been suggested that financing or stabilization would assist farmers in need. Mr. Speaker, we financed special loans at 12 per cent interest when the interest rate was 16 per cent or 18 per cent. We subsidized that interest rate by four points. We have seen what the Provinces did for producers who depend on the great free market to give them a proper return.
Our agricultural bill is ASA-it is a kind of aspirin for a very sick market. And that is what it is, Mr. Speaker, a sick market. It does not give the efficient producer a sufficient return for him to pay his bills. The producers say they do not want any handouts. The Hon. Member who presented the motion complained that I am not going ahead with stabilization as quickly as I should. He said that the Provinces have offered a plan. Mr. Speaker, it is a plan similar to the one I offered to them in 1977, so that is tremendous progress! 1 do not know if you want to call that progressive conservatism, but it certainly is not liberalism.
1 offered that plan to them in Yorkton, Saskatchewan, at a federal-provincial ministers' meeting. It was a 100 per cent guaranteed income assurance. The Provinces said no and the producers said no. They said this wild man Whelan was offering concessions to producers that would cause overproduction and all kinds of things that they did not want. What do you think they are suggesting now, Mr. Speaker? They go so far as to say that I should pay a producer on as high as 12,000 head of swine or 16,000 head of cattle. They say that is how the Agricultural Stabilization Act should be. That means that the lawyers on the fifteenth, sixteenth and twentieth floors could be producers-vertical integration in a massive form, is what they are suggesting. I can tell you right now, Mr. Speaker, that I am not going for that massive figure they have suggested.
We have taken part in every meeting since June. Last fall they told me that if I did not have anything for them, they would have something for me by July 1. I told them to go ahead and present me with something. The Provinces were going to work in harmony, in a peaceful, constructive attitude and I thought that was fine. I had offered them something and only one Province thought it could support me. The Minister from Ontario said he would support me but he never got the official support of his Government. Then a new Minister of Agriculture in Ontario said that if we were not going to do it he would do it. I told him to go ahead. The Provinces worked together for pretty nearly a year but only four of them said they were in favour of some kind of plan. I thought that was pretty good because I did not expect ten of them to agree on anything at any time.
The Canadian Pork Council, which represents every Province, said it wanted the same thing for pork, but the provincial Ministers do not say that they will come in. How can we have a national plan if only four Provinces support one commodity? It has been suggested that this is a voluntary program, a dollar from the producers, a dollar from the Provinces and a dollar from the federal Government in order to build up a fund. But some producers do not have a dollar. We would have to sign a contract with them to the effect that when they sell their product, whether it be a lamb, a pig, a calf, a finished animal or whatever, we would deduct the first premium from the cost. That is the only way they would be able to participate in the plan at the present time. We used that principle in the crop insurance program. Some of the farmers could never get a dollar from the banks.
The Hon. Member who proposed the motion condemned the Farm Credit Corporation but, Mr. Speaker, his Party condemns Crown corporations right and left. Does he not realize that there are other lending institutions in the country that have a responsibility to lend in rural Canada also? In 1976 we asked the lending institutions if they would lend money to farmers. They said they would and that they would participate in long-term mortgages. I can show you records, Mr. Speaker, of farmers who thought they had long-term records but really had nothing but a piece of paper which, at the will and fancy of the manager of the bank, could be turned into a floating note. That is what happened in many cases. When farmers thought they had a loan at 1 I per cent it jumped to 24 per cent.
The Hon. Member for Bruce-Grey (Mr. Gurbin) knows very well that when we were lending money at 16 per cent, those farmers were being taken off the hook because banks were charging them 22 per cent or 23 per cent. We were lending at 16 per cent. Hon. Members opposite forget that we subsidized those farmers for two years, down to 12 per cent which no lending institution, other than the Farm Credit Corporation, would give for any kind of long-term money. I challenge any Hon. Members to come forward and show me a lending institution today which would give a farmer a 20-year mortgage. That is what the Farm Credit Corporation is doing. We are giving a 20-year mortgage with a fixed interest rate for
October 21, 1983

the first ten years. If any Hon. Members can get a fixed interest rate for longer than three years from any bank or lending institution, I ask him to bring it forward and present it in this House.
Are Hon. Members opposite suggesting to me that the Farm Credit Corporation should be the total lender for the whole agriculture industry? It seems to be that way, because this year we have put up the largest amount of money we have ever loaned in Canada under the Farm Credit Corporation, a corporation which Members opposite have spent days in this House condemning-a terrible thing, they say, which is going to swallow up the whole nation.
We are told we are not aiding agriculture in Saskatchewan-which has that good Conservative Government-yet they sold 500 Hereford heifers to a terrible system, Bulgaria, a Communist system, and we assembled the cattle for them free. We did all the testing for them free. We made sure the cattle got to Sherbrooke, Quebec. Our Canadian veterinarians went to Bulgaria on the boat. And how did they sell them out of Saskatchewan? Through ADCO, a Crown corporation which is used for export in Saskatchewan. According to the newspapers, the Premier of Saskatchewan is going to enter into a contract with Communist China. It will be a partner with good old Conservative Saskatchewan for $500 million in a joint potash operation. I find it funny. 1 find it hypocritical also. At election time these countries are condemned. The feds are condemned for even talking trade with these countries.
Not too many days ago an Hon. Member in this House condemned us for being friendly with Cuba, saying that Cuba was the Prime Minister's friend. We sell to Cuba a lot of agriculture products, and they have paid for every one of them on the barrelhead. Last year we did $340 million worth of trade with Cuba. It pays. We are not supposed to assist Cuba in agriculture and trade with it. Not only the Premier of Saskatchewan but the Premier of Alberta was in China. The Premier of Ontario was in Indonesia and all over South East Asia. The Minister of Agriculture of British Columbia is over in Europe. He is going to be visiting many of the same countries we trade with. He is going to improve trade. How are these governments doing it? They are doing it with Crown corporations because that is the only way they can trade with some of those countries.
Canagrex, which could have been in business two years ago had it been allowed to go through this House, could have improved trade because there is no other nation of agricultural producers which depends so much on trade as we do. Some 50 per cent of our income comes from trade. Last year our biggest sale ever of grain, over 29 million metric tonnes, moved out of this country into trade. Our exports of agricultural products last year went up 12 per cent. In the United States of America, which gives all kinds of concessions, exports of agricultural products went down 12 per cent. The U.S. had great interest-free concessions, charitable repayment plans, which we did not even involve ourselves in because Canada has the respect of the
Supply
world, and these people understand that when they go trading.
I am talking about the Farm Credit Corporation, the NEED Program and so on.
Let us not forget that under the Constitution agriculture is a joint responsibility. That should be made very plain and clear. The Official Opposition agriculture critic comes from the Province of Manitoba where we spend twice as much money assisting farmers with programs than the Province of Manitoba ever did under an NDP or Conservative government. That government never spent the proportion of money we do.
We spend more than twice as much on agriculture in the Province of Saskatchewan than the provincial government does. Yet the Premier has funds to appoint a trade minister to run all over the world. We do not do it in Alberta because Alberta has the Heritage Fund, and it is saying it is cutting back on irrigation plans and so on. What the PFRA spends in the Province of Saskatchewan, for instance, does keep rural municipalities alive. In the last ten years we spent $33 million in small towns and villages for sewage systems and water reservoirs. We funded 50 per cent and we gave an outright grant for the other 50 per cent. The Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Association is one of the best organizations ever created in this country, and it should be there for all of Canada.
We have been told we are slow in British Columbia in the matter of stabilization and how much money we are spending. I met with the farmers in British Columbia. I went with an Hon. Member of the Opposition from that area and talked to farmers. The Minister of Agriculture in British Columbia did not suggest any tariffs, as some Hon. Member said. He said to me at a meeting: "We are not suggesting tariffs because they might reciprocate on lumber and we ship a lot of lumber into the great United States of America". So we are subject to this type of importation and all the different kinds of trade problems.
I am sure the Hon. Member knows what is going on in the United States now. There is a hearing being conducted. We hope the decision will be handed down in November. Potatoes going into the United States from the Maritimes have an extra 17-cent tariff tacked on because little New Brunswick and little Prince Edward Island are going to destroy the great potato industry in New England. The U.S. says this is because the federal Minister of Agriculture has such superior programs that it cannot compete with us.
I received a letter from a person representing the Canadian Horticultural Society. He comes from the Province of Manitoba. It did this Minister's heart good to hear him tell in glowing terms about the great job that was being done, and how the Secretary for Agriculture in	the	United	States	is not payingany attention. Right now in	the United	States	of America alaw has been passed through its	Senate	which	will limit theimportation of beef. It has	not	gone through	its Congress.
Because there is no control on dairy production, those farmers are scared to death that what the Secretary for Agriculture is going to do in dairy production will cause over a million dairy cows to be slaughtered. These cows are producing nutritious food which could be distributed all over the world, ft is

suggested they be slaughtered because the U.S. has a straight subsidy program, a very high subsidy program, which does not have any control over production.
The efficient American dairy farmers just produced and produced and now there are nearly 700,000 metric tonnes of surplus skim milk powder. There are over 320,000 metric tonnes of surplus butter. They do not know what to do with it. They are taking some of our markets because the U.S. is a much bigger economic power than we are. It says it is not. Let us use Jamaica as an example. This is a country to which we supplied skim milk powder for years. It trades dairy products, mainly powder, for bauxite. We do not need that in Canada so it trades with the U.S. In Mexico, the U.S. sold 60,000 tonnes of skim milk powder and gave them 20,000 tonnes of food aid. They said that did not lower the price, but that is questionable as far as I am concerned.
I would like to speak about research for a moment. Poultry production owes its reputation for being so efficient in the world to Agriculture Canada research, which developed a serum so that instead of losing one-third of your poultry flock through a normal laying span, you lose less than half of one per cent. Never did our chickens lay so much and do so much for society. It used to take almost an hour's wages to buy one dozen eggs. In Canada today, because of efficiency and the longevity of the chicken, and because of productivity, one hour's average industrial wage will buy the average Canadian a year's supply of eggs. The average Canadian eats 12 dozen eggs per year. The average industrial wage is $12 per hour, and the average price for a dozen eggs in Canada today is one dollar. We are the envy of the whole world.
This will be our largest year for exporting pure-bred Holstein cattle. These exports have expanded and expanded. It will be our largest year for exporting semen, exporting grain.
I could go on and on telling you the things we have done in agriculture. The Hon. Member says I have not done anything. We put 14 new programs into effect since 1 have been in agriculture and we only added 26 man-years to Agriculture Canada. The Auditor General has commended the Agriculture Department for the tremendous job it has done.
I could go on and talk about interest-free advance payments. The Hon. Member says he does not want handouts, but there are these interest-free advance payments, and not only with the Wheat Board. Last year there was nearly $500 million in interest-free advance payments, yet they say we are not doing anything. I will just close by saying that nothing is so firmly believed but that which is least known.

Mr. Speaker, it almost sounds as thought the Minister was rereading one of the speeches of Mr. Gardiner in Saskatchewan 20 years ago. His figures do not add up today. If you look at the $6 billion of profit the farmers have added to this country and compare that with 1.25 per cent of the budget attributed to agriculture, it is a pretty sick figure. That is all I have to say about that speech.

I could comment a little bit about that. I am really glad that the Hon. Member mentioned the late Jimmy Gardiner, who was the Minister of Agriculture in Canada for 22 years. He was from Saskatchewan and he did more for agriculture than probably anyone else. He understood agriculture, which is something the Hon. Member does not understand.
The Hon. Member is contracting his colleague because his colleague said it is not money that makes for a healthy agriculture. He is saying we should spend more money. Some of the countries spending more money than us do not have as healthy an agricultural industry as we do.
We have programs in this country which will allow farmers to receive a decent price in the marketplace if they want to organize themselves. I think he is suggesting, Mr. Speaker, that we pour millions and millions more dollars into agriculture and that is going to be its salvation. I am sure he does not mean that at all because I am told his own operation does not depend on Government handouts. I am sure that if he wanted to give you his account books, he would be in that 50 per cent bracket I talked about-the people who do not owe a penny.

Mr. Speaker, in his comments the Minister said that all that the farmers want is a decent profit. That being the case, they must be able to meet their expenses and I agree with that. I would like to ask the Minister why he was not able to get through Cabinet a formula agreed to by his Government and the egg producers, namely that their input costs would be met? Why was he not able to get through Cabinet that the input costs farmers face be subject to six and five?

Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member does not know what went through Cabinet. I do not think he does. We are just dealing with it this week and I am sure he would be very surprised at what went through Cabinet. But I am not at liberty to tell him at this time.
I am really happy that the Hon. Member for Provencher (Mr. Epp) is so supportive of marketing boards. I hope you have that from your Party caucus and your Leader. I continually get people saying "Wait until we change the Government and we will get rid of all of them".
No, you never heard that from this side of the House.

I get letters on this. You do not know what impression you have planted in people's minds. Yet the Hon. Member is supporting the marketing boards, which I have supported. I say as humbly as 1 can that probably the Hon. Member would not even be asking questions if I had not supported the Canadian Egg Marketing Agency when it was so controversial. Most Prime Ministers would have said that is too controversial and would get it out of here. But the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) said to me: "Mr. Minister, as long as they are doing things honestly and so on and you say that you are doing it properly, I will back you". I am now glad I have the backing of the Hon. Member for Provencher.
October 21, 1983

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: I would want to recognize the Hon. Member to give him an opportunity to enter into questions, answers and comments but I have to recognize him on a point of order.

Mr. Speaker, the Conservative policy has been misstated. This is not debate, it is merely a statement of fact. The Conservative policy has been that marketing boards, when it is the wish of the farmer, shall be organized, respected and assisted. But there shall be no compulsion from an arrogant Minister to force any group of farmers at any point in time to form themselves into a marketing board.

The Hon. Member could not find any time that I forced anyone into a marketing board. I have suggested this to them. If the Hon. Member wanted to do some good, he could go down to his own Province. They are asking me now to spend millions of dollars because the marketplace has not returned a decent profit to potato producers in his own Province. We have spent millions and millions on stabilization and he knows it. I would like to see that Party's policy, and I hope the Hon. Member will send it to me, the official Party policy which supports marketing boards.

Mr. Speaker, I agree with the Minister when he says things humbly. I agree that he has a lot to be humble about and I am glad he recognizes that.
Just to support and elaborate a little on what the Hon. Member for Carleton-Charlotte (Mr. McCain) said, he is precisely right in stating our position on marketing boards. Let me go further and say there are ways other than compulsion to form marketing boards. I sat in a room with this Minister some seven or eight years ago when he used coercion and other things to-
Friendly persuasion.

It is one thing to use friendly persuasion; it is another thing to take an industry when it is down and say: "You are not going to have anything from me unless you agree with me on supply management". That is where we on this side disagree. The Minister may want to use coercion and compulsion, although it may not be compulsion in his mind, but when you find a producer in a very bad financial situation, it in fact becomes compulsion. We do not agree with kicking people when they are down. We like to help people so they do not find themselves in a bad financial position.
Very specifically, is the Minister in favour of reducing the tax on farm fuels in order ot keep producers' cost of production down? There is another way of getting returns from the marketplace which satisfy your expenses and that is by reducing the expenses. Is this Minister in favour of reducing-I did not say eliminating-the federal Government tax on farm fuel?

The Hon. Member has talked about coercion. I challenge him on what he said. I may use moral suasion on people, tell them the benefits of marketing boards and their participation, but I have never suggested to anyone that there
Supply
would be any action taken which would be coercion. Not this Minister of Agriculture. 1 have been elected to office since I was 21 years of age and I know about democracy.
The Hon. Member talks about fuel taxes. Earlier he said that he did not want handouts. The marketplace is the place to get the return for farmers. For instance, canola seed has gone up, what, 40 per cent since July? That is the seed. Meal has gone up 42 per cent and the oil has gone up 92 per cent. He never mentioned in his speech about how rapidly the market can change. That has more effect on farmers. But what he is saying is: "Whelan, you must have programs that guarantee that when the free market system gets sick, you must be the doctor who comes in with the proper medicine to make sure it gets healthy again".
We know there are marketing people in this country to whom I have not given a penny of aid since 1972, and when there was another government here for a short term, it did not give them a penny of aid either. That is the poultry industry all the way through. We have not changed our aid to the dairy industry for over seven years. If you find me one of those efficient producers in that bracket who are going broke, I would be very surprised.

Mr. Speaker, I have a very short intervention. It seems to me that there is perhaps some logic to the Minister saying that he has not implemented changes to the stabilization program because it requires the consent of the Provinces and he does not have a program along the East Coast for potato producers to form a marketing board because he must rely on the assistance of the Provinces.
However, there is one area which is strictly within his own jurisdiction but in which he has not been acting very quickly. I refer to putting the personnel in place for Canagrex. He had plenty of time when the Canagrex legislation was in its various stages of debate to hold the interviews and make the preparations. How long must we wait for the people who will be appointed to Canagrex?

First, Mr. Speaker, I was not that optimistic that Canagrex would ever be passed. I think it would have been very wrong for me to interview people and say: "You are going to be hired for Canagrex". I did not do anything until after Parliament finally passed it into law. We hired Peat Marwick to do headhunting for us and put ads in the papers, and I made my recommendations to the Government about three weeks ago.
