Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to rise and speak on this motion put forward today because of the serious situation in which farmers find themselves with regard to present cash flow problems.
The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) who finished his remarks just before lunch made the point that agriculture and farmers had been very progressive throughout the years and I agree with that. They have been very productive in terms of their input into Canada's economy, being $8 billion to $9 billion; but I do not agree when the Minister said it was because of what the Government did. Basically, that is what I heard him say, that producers were so productive. In fact, the opposite is true. It is in spite of the lack of policy and direction with regard to agriculture that farmers have produced and have been productive.
I want to talk about some matters today, hopefully in a positive sense so that we can have an adjustment of some very serious problems that exist for the producers. First is one which has been mentioned by other Members, the Western Grain Stabilization Program. That Program came into existence in 1976. There was a small payout. When the Hon. Otto Lang introduced that program, it was on the basis that it was not to be crop insurance but a program that would deal with the cash flow problems of farmers.
Let us face the situation as it exists. This Program has not dealt with this problem of the farmers. However, the Government has $860 million of farmers' money in the treasury somewhere. By the middle of January it is projected that the Government will have over $1 billion of farmers' money. I see the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) in the House this afternoon. I contend that the Government is playing politics with farmers' money.
We remember that farmers first paid in $500, which was deducted at the elevator at the time they delivered their grain. Then it was increased to $900, and last year there was a further increase to $1,200. If a farmer got into the plan in 1979 and made no payment since, he would have paid in $4,800, that is, if he paid the maximum. Had he invested that amount of money in a bank at prime interest rates, he would
have accumulated $7,124. Just by depositing that money in the bank, the farmer would have had some $7,124 to be used in his cash flow. Yet the Minister rises in the House and tells Canadians what a great job the Government has done. I want to set the record straight. It has done great job of hanging on to the farmers' money, every cent of which the primary producer deposited at his own cost into a program to enhance and benefit the farmer when he had major cash flow problems.
1 am glad the Minister is present. He must deal with this situation and take some positive steps toward helping farmers. Let us deal with the problem. I contend that the Government and the Minister of Agriculture are playing politics here.
Can you imagine?
I hear the Minister. About two months before the election there is nothing more they would like to do than to write out a nice little cheque. What I am trying to do-
What are you doing?

I am trying to bring about some responsible action. The way this can be done is simple. The program has to be adjusted. It is not working on a five-year, retroactive basis. The formula does not add up.
Why isn't it working?

The Minister of Agriculture is heckling me because I have hit a very sensitive spot.
It is most important that the Government deal with this issue. I meet with my farmers weekly. They are saying that the program should either be cleaned up or they should be let out of it. They cannot afford to pay $1,200. They have to pay their fuel and grocery bills. They have to pay machine costs, and they are faced with a major cash flow problem at this time.
1 ask the Minister to carry this representation concerning the very serious problem in grain stabilization to Cabinet and to the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau). The Prime Minister suggested to the House that because there was no representation in western Canada, basically speaking in agricultural areas, he would make a special effort to deal with the problems, the presentations and the representations that were made. The Minister of Agriculture owes it to western producers to look into the Western Grain Stabilization Program.
Another area of cash flow problems about which the Government could do something very positive is the initial price of grain. What is its history? On almost a daily basis I have contacted the Canadian Wheat Board to discover that the asking price of wheat, going back to January of this year, has been 99 cents to $1 per bushel higher than what farmers are receiving as an initial price delivered at the grain elevator. In the case of Durum, I obtained figures from the Wheat Board yesterday indicating that the asking price was $2.10 per bushel higher. Farmers were pleased to see an increase in the initial price of barley. Today it is selling at $140 per tonne in Thunder Bay.
October 21, 1983
And higher in Vancouver.

Yes, it is even higher in Vancouver. The Government should take some positive steps to increase the cash flow position of farmers. All it has to do is give them their money and increase the initial price of wheat, as well as the initial price of Durum. Most responsible people in the grain trade will say that 50 cents per bushel is adequate leeway or an adequate holdback within the Canadian Wheat Board to deal with problems that may arise. Certainly the Minister could recommend to Cabinet that the initial price of wheat and of Durum be increased by 50 cents per bushel.
As I indicated earlier, this is the farmers' money. They are not asking for handouts. The Minister said today that he was handing out money for this and that to farmers. In comparison with the contribution that agriculture makes to the country, farmers are being short-changed in terms of the budget which goes through this place. I pointed this out to the Minister earlier, and he walked all the way around it. In fact, farmers are being considered only in about 1.25 per cent of the entire budget of the country. He knows that those figures are accurate. The Government could take some positive direction in the area of western grain stabilization. There could be improvement in the initial price of grain which would in turn improve the cash flow of farmers.
Instead of giving, the Government is taking. It has placed an excessive farm fuel tax on diesel fuel and other fuels used for the production of food. The Government has a direct federal tax of 77 cents per gallon on farm fuels. That is very excessive. On December 13, 1979 when we were defeated, it was a bad day-
A bad day for Canada.
Yes, it was a bad day for Canada. At that time the price of fuel in the little village of Macoun-is Mr. Speaker, indicating that my time is up?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Yes.
Perhaps you could seek unanimous consent.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Is there unanimous consent for the Hon. Member to continue his remarks?
Agreed.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: There appears to be unanimous consent.

Thank you, Mr. Speaker. I will make my comments short. As I was saying, on December 13, 1979 in the little village of Macoun the price of fuel was 98 cents per gallon. I recall that day. It was a rather dark day for a new Member who had been defeated. Today the price of fuel is close to $2 per gallon.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Order. I would like to inform the Hon. Member that the Chair was in error. He had 20 minutes in total, of which he has ten remaining.

It is important to have this heavy-handed farm fuel tax removed. The Minister has said that the Government has made contributions to farmers, but farmers have been paying heavy-handed taxes to the Government on farm fuel. This is counterproductive for farmers. Many of them are not working. Many of them are not involved in summer fallow because they simply cannot afford it. It costs $150 to fill the fuel tank of a tractor. This will reflect in the cost of production. Have the Minister and the Government considered removing some of this tax on the farmers in order that they can be as productive as they have been in the past and even improve upon that?
I wish to deal with another area where this Government has long promised to move but has failed to do so. I refer to the capital gains tax on farmers. Members may ask what that has to do with cash flow. It has a lot to do with it. Let me give an example.
A father may ask his son for a reasonable sum of money for his land in order that he may retire with some dignity in a small town after years of hard work. The young farmer will do it so that his father may live with respectability. At that point the father is expected to pay capital gains tax to the Government of Canada. It becomes restrictive. Again and again in this House, as recently as two weeks ago, we have called upon the Government to remove the capital gains tax on farms, but nothing has been done to this point.
In the last three elections the Government promised to make moves in this direction, but it has failed to do so. It is my hope that the Minister of Agriculture will ask Cabinet to look into the capital gains tax on farms, which is very restrictive and counterproductive to agriculture.
The Minister had something to say about farm credit, as he does from time to time. There are some solutions to the farm credit problem. There is not enough money in the fund. More important, the rate is far too high. Young farmers cannot afford to borrow at those high rates. Our Party has proposed a way to get around this. There are farmers who would invest their money in an agri-bond. Young farmers would receive the benefit of that investment. They would be able to borrow from that fund to finance their farm. We made this suggestion some time ago and the Minister is well aware of it. The Government has failed to act in a positive way in regard to financing for farmers. This would facilitate the situation as at present the needs of young farmers are not being met.
The Minister talked about how much money the federal Government was paying to the Provinces. However, he failed to mention the great contribution by agriculture through taxation to central Canada, particularly the bureaucracy. The farmers are not happy with the way the Government spends their hard-earned money. They make that clear to us.
I now want to deal with another important point. 1 have contended for some time that there seem to be different standards for different areas of production. That is not right. The farmer has many expenses, such as machinery and fuel

October 21, 1983
Supply
bills. After meeting his expenses, he should be able to have a good standard of living for himself and his family. However, according to the Tax Department and other sources, the average net income of a farmer is approximately $4,000. Compare this to the fact that a consumer spends about 15 per cent of his earnings on food. That is a rather dynamic result from the production of our primary producers. It is most important that this continue.
Our farmers are proud that they can produce cheap food for Canadians. In return, it is only fair that this Government not penalize our producers. Farmers should not be discouraged from contributing in such a positive way.
The latest move by this Government with regard to the statutory Crow rate will result in very high freight rates. This will cause major problems. I was aghast when the Minister of Transport (Mr. Axworthy) rose to impose closure on Bill C-155, the statutory Crow rate. He is inflicting upon the farmers freight rate increases at a time when they cannot afford it. No consideration is being given to the cash flow problems of the farmer.
I see you rising, Mr. Speaker. Thank you for the opportunity to put forward briefly some of our concerns regarding agriculture. I hope that the Government, and the Minister of Agriculture in particular, will lend an ear to some of the recommendations we have made which will result in a positive effect on agriculture in the future.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Are Hon. Members rising to ask questions? If not, the Chair will recognize the Hon. Member for Lambton-Middlesex (Mr. Ferguson).

Mr. Speaker, I am delighted to take part in this debate. 1 commend the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) for the firm direction he has given to this vital renewable resource as he enters into his eleventh year, except for a brief sabbatical, as Minister of Agriculture for Canada. He has given us the direction and legislation we have needed to make the Canadian farmer one of the most efficient and productive in any country of the world.
I have to take issue with some of the comments made by previous speakers who have suggested that the tri-party stabilization programs are the answer to all our problems. For a few years I belonged to a program. In the Province of Ontario there was a joint program between the producers and the provincial Government. The producers paid in an equal amount to the Ontario Government for a cow-calf stabilization program that seemed at the beginning to be an excellent program. In fact, in the first three years of the program we received a payout because the price received was not comparable to that of the cost of production. However, in the fourth year of the program we all realized that there would be no payout, but many of us sent in our premiums regardless. However, that program was cancelled in the fourth year because less than half of the farmers involved had sent in their premiums. Consequently, the program collapsed.
[DOT] (M30)
I would hope that if we are to proceed with a stabilization program for the red meat sector, there will be guarantees built in to make it compulsory for the producer to sign up and to remain a part of that program for the required number of years. The producer should not simply sign up when prices are low and ride out the peak times when prices are good. I believe, however, that farm stabilization programs are not the answer.
When looking at methods used to establish a price discovery mechanism for many of the products produced in Canada which do not fall under the jurisdiction of the marketing agencies, we have to realize that there must be a counterbalance or a countervailing force in the marketplace. Last week, for example, the price of soybeans on the Chicago futures market had dropped by approximately 75 cents per bushel. Soybean futures dropped that much in spite of the fact that a week ago yesterday a United States Department of Agriculture report pointed out that supplies of soybeans needed to carry us through to the next crop year would perhaps be inadequate to meet the demand. If that was the case, why did the price drop last week? I submit, Mr. Speaker, that the system has broken down and that it is only through a system of establishing a price at the farm gate that reflects the cost of production to the efficient producer that we can overcome this problem.
Since we have such large requirements for capital in the farming sector at the present time, I submit to you, Sir, that the solution could be found if the national marketing agencies which are in existence at the present time, whether through dairy, poultry or another commodity, were to have price setting mechanisms that reflected the cost of production of the efficient producer and if they were to be under the jurisdiction of a supervisory body so that the interests of the consumer are also protected. No company can operate without a return on investment, management and risk. Consequently, farming is no longer a way of life; rather, it is big business and we must have these guarantees built in if it is to be successful.
No amount of funding, whether from the Farm Credit Corporation or any other body, will relieve the situation if we do not first cure the problem of the price at the farm gate to the farmer. I suggest that to increase the amount of funding available through the Farm Credit Corporation would perhaps be a short-term solution, but the producer cannot borrow himself out of trouble. There must be a return from the marketplace that reflects that cost to the producer and then there must be a reasonable markup to the packer or processor and to the retailer. Finally, most important of all, there must be a fair price to the consumer.
My colleagues have been speaking about the need for agribonds and I do not quarrel with that need. I believe there is a place for agri-bonds but I do not think they go far enough. For example, what if a father wanted to turn the family farm over to his son? Many of us began farming with the assistance of our fathers who loaned us machinery for those first crucial years of farming so that we did not have to make huge cash
October 21, 1983

outlays. Many of us received an interest rate on mortgages well below the current rate from our fathers. Under the agri-bond system, this is not possible.
I submit, Mr. Speaker, that we must come up with a different provision to maintain the family farm, which is recognized as the most efficient production unit in the world today. I submit we must come up with a different proposal to guarantee a mortgage, if the farmer in fact took one back on his fixed capital assets, on the sale of his enterprise to a member of his family. I maintain that this is essential if the family farm is to continue to be the backbone of the Canadian agriculture sector. We need provisions to allow the farmer the flexibility to give a member of his family a reduced rate of interest in order to give him a start, so that he can build up an operation, achieve a level of equity that puts him on a secure footing and which allows him to proceed to contribute to the industry that is so important to the economy of the country.
The lending of the Farm Credit Corporation in itself tells a story about what is required in the agricultural sector. We should look at the number of farmers who are in arrears to the Farm Credit Corporation and look back to see in which sector of the agricultural industry they are involved. We would recognize immediately that those farmers involved in the red meat sector form the largest percentage of those in arrears. Grain farmers come next. The reason for this is that these are the producers who do not have the power to set their prices at the farm gate. They have to rely on the vagaries of the marketplace as well as the vagaries of mother nature. This creates the type of speculation that is taking place today on the commodity futures market. There certainly is no security there for any of the farmers who need this money so badly.
Another situation that has occurred over the last several years is that the number of retail food outlets has dropped dramatically. The fact is that five retail food chains control 75 per cent of the retail food outlets in Canada. Those five chains have in turn banded together to form buying groups to exert even more pressure on the marketplace. Consequently, there is the need for an even greater countervailing force in the marketplace than the national marketing agencies can provide. It is in this context that I hope the producers of Canada will take advantage of the legislation available to them not only at the provincial level but also at the federal level to give them the type of income that is commensurate with that of the rest of society and to protect their investments. This is essential if we are to have a healthy agricultural industry in Canada.
As I look further at the type of federal assistance that exists for the farmers in Canada, I see that there is assistance not only through the Farm Credit Corporation but assistance is also provided to the vegetable producers and the fruit growers to ensure that there are adequate supplies of fresh Canadian fruits and vegetables available to Canadians. The vegetable cold storage program has been utilized across Canada to a great extent. We have a large number of programs that are not recognized by many Members of Parliament. There is the grain storage program under which money can be borrowed from the Government interest-free on grain held in storage to
Supply
allow it to go to the marketplace in an orderly fashion. They are all very positive programs. The fact remains, however, that there is a provincial responsibility that must be used in co-ordination with the federal programs.
The Minister of Agriculture has had a great deal of involvement in research and ours is among the best in the world. We have the highest quality food of any country and we have the highest standards of any country. Consequently, even though the budget of the Department of Agriculture is lower than some of us would like it to be, it reflects the lean, hard image portrayed by the Minister himself.
Even the Minister is smiling at that!
There is no fat in the Department.
Lean, mean Gene.

It has a lean, hard image which reflects the position we have taken over the years that we have to trim off the fat. We must make sure that we recognize the latest methods of production so that we can keep abreast or ahead of the rest of the world in the marketplace.
When we compare yields of the various crops, we see that in Canada, and particularly in Ontario, our average production per acre is higher than that of the United States, whether it be in soybeans or corn. I think it is interesting that we have this potential productivity.
I want to reflect now on the increased productivity that has taken place through research and development and marketing agencies. Many people say that our system of planned production through marketing boards leads to inefficiencies. The figures show otherwise, Mr. Speaker. A few years ago a laying hen would produce approximately 20 dozen eggs in any one-year laying cycle; now the production is 24 dozen per bird. The number of pounds of feed necessary to produce a dozen eggs has decreased as well. As the Minister said this morning, the mortality rate has decreased. This is an example of the efficiencies that have come about. Although the price is set according to the cost of production, if the farmer can be more efficient than average, he can increase his margin of profit. This has happened and he has become more efficient in the process.
A number of buyers from other countries come to my constituency. Recently a buyer came from Russia to buy dairy cattle. Some of the best productivity records in the world are held by Canadian producers. Some of these cattle are used to increase the number of offspring of one select animal by way of embryo transplant. One mother can mother six or eight offspring in one year and the embryo can be transplanted into a host cow.
When you have a man as busy and who does such a good job as the Minister of Agriculture, it would be nice if we could clone him and have two of him.

October 21, 1983
Supply
Whether Canadians are farmers or are engaged in the agri-food industry as a veterinarian, say, they have been leaders in research in spite of the fact that the budget is not as great as that of many other countries. This just shows the ingenuity and imagination of the people involved in this sector. We can look at its accomplishments with pride. Well within the span of my lifetime one farmer fed eight people; now one farmer feeds 70 people. Of course, I am talking about southwestern Ontario. That part of Ontario that lies west of a line drawn between Georgian Bay and Toronto produces about 20 per cent of all agricultural production in Canada on a dollar basis. Through the greenhouse industry and intensified farming practices it has a higher rate of productivity than other areas of the country. Climatic conditions contribute to production as well, because in that area it is unusual to have a crop failure or to suffer the drought that sometimes happens in other parts of Canada.
The federal Government has met its responsibilities not only in the area of food production but also in research, plant health programs and inspection programs. I recently received a call from a show in Cologne, Germany, asking us to supply 600 tonnes of turkey. The largest turkey hatchery in the world is in my riding and it has branches in the United States. It supplies 22 per cent of the North American market and 11 per cent of the world market. It is a very sophisticated Canadian operation and is a family business. Through research and assistance from the Department of Agriculture they have been able to raise their production to the standards required to break into the world market. This is a credit to the Canadian Department of Agriculture and to Canadian farmers.
Through the PIK program in the United States this year they tried to take land out of production and a drought followed. This has not happened in Canada with our programs. There has been drought and adverse weather conditions in some areas of the country but we do not have a PIK program. One has to question the morality of such a program for Canada when there are so many hungry nations in the world. Our programs are tailored to meet the demand of the domestic and export markets. The crop year in grain production is tailored so that none of the product is actually sold prior to leaving the farm. When it leaves the farm we know that it is on the way to market.
During the hearings on the Crow rate I could not help but think that ours has to be one of the most efficient systems in the world. The cost to the producer is well within his means and he can afford to get his crop to market, especially with assistance from the Government.

Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the Hon. Member for Lambton-Middlesex (Mr. Ferguson). I made a note of the enormous efficiencies he has claimed that have taken place in the farming community in recent years. I should like to ask him how it is that a farmer today can feed 70 people and yet he himself starves.

Mr. Speaker, I am sorry the Hon. Member has missed the point I was making. Those farmers who have orderly marketing systems are making a reasonable return on their investment and a reasonable return for management and risk. If the other parts of our agricultural sector would take advantage of the programs which are available to them-the meat sector and some of the grain sectors-to establish the price at the farm gate, then they could also enjoy the same level of prosperity as those who have their marketing agencies operative and in place.

Mr. Speaker, just so I have that question on the record, could we take it, then, that the position of the Liberal Members is that there should be marketing boards for the beef industry? Is that the position of the Government?

Mr. Speaker, regarding the beef industry I should point out, being a beef producer myself-and I have been for a lot more years than I care to remember, well over 35 years-that is one part of our operation which is certainly not showing a profit. I started out as a beef producer when I was 14 years old. I was a 4H Club member. I bought a heifer calf and built up a herd. I am very proud of that herd, but in an economic sense I should have sold it quite a few years ago. However, I do have scrub land across part of my home farm and if I am going to scavenge the pasture off that land, I have to keep some cattle. It is not a profitable venture.
1 am suggesting there is a way that we can bring a reasonable return to the beef producers of Canada. I would like to suggest to the Hon. Member that we allow our feedlot operators to fill up to capacity, and base this on cost of production. However, rather than feeding those steers out to 1,250 pounds to 1,300 pounds, what is wrong with selling them 50 pounds lighter than that if the demand is not there? By so doing we would tailor our production to the marketplace to reflect the demand, whether domestic or export.
These are my own ideas and thoughts on the matter. I am not sure what the Minister of Agriculture thinks about it. I believe he would agree with me that it is a great idea. I feel it would solve a lot of problems in the red meat sector if we had a system like this, where a person could set their price at the farm gate rather than have the existing conditions continue. The spread between the wholesaler and consumer in Montreal a year ago last August was 41 cents a pound greater than a similar spread in the United States. Someone is ripping off the marketplace, and I suggest to you it is not the farmer but someone further up the ladder. If the farmer was even getting half of that spread, he would be making a profit.

Mr. Speaker, it quite amazes me that the Hon. Member can claim to be associated with 4H Clubs and, after that number of years of pledging his head to clearer thinking, would still join the Liberal Party.
I still ask him whether it is or is not the policy of the Government of Canada today to have beef marketing boards for the sale of beef. 1 believe that was the answer he applied to
October 21, 1983

my first question. If that was the answer, I want him to say definitively whether or not he and his Party are trying to have a system of marketing boards for the beef industry. I want a yes or no answer for the record.

Mr. Speaker, there is no way I can speak on behalf of the Minister of Agriculture. However, as a person who has spent so many years in the beef industry, I know what the needs of that industry are, and my personal opinion is, after losing money for several years, that there has to be a better way. Being a Liberal and a pragmatist as well, I am willing to try something new. If that is the only way left, then I am willing to give it a try. However, I am not going to be hamstrung by some old fashioned thinking that there is a free enterprise system left in the marketplace today where we have various types of monopolies in existence.

Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member for Lambton-Middlesex (Mr. Ferguson) used the word "tailored" several times during his address. I would suggest that he meant to say "Whelaned". Had the agricultural policy of this country been "Taylored", agriculture would not be in the mess it is in today!
1 would like to ask the Hon. Member a question in connection with egg production. The egg producers of Alberta are now having a very difficult time. They have co-operated 100 per cent with the Government in the six and five program. They are now up to the six and five ceiling, but the production costs have kept on increasing. Production costs are now between 4 per cent and 5 per cent above what the producers are able to charge, because they have reached their limit under the six and five program. These egg producers are unable to carry that burden, which simply means that if something is not done to provide the egg producers with the opportunity of increasing their price, they are going to go into bankruptcy. Has the Hon. Member for Lambton-Middlesex any comment as to what the Government might be able to do to keep these producers viable?

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to respond to that question because I have been following the problem very closely. 1 am glad to see the Hon. Member has tailored his thinking along the lines of the marketing boards. I am also very much aware that the marketing board people were the first to endorse the six and five program. During my address I spoke about the vagaries of the marketplace and what is happening on the Chicago futures exchange. In fact, the price of feed has increased by 23 per cent since last June. That is well beyond the capability of the egg producer to cope with, I quite agree with the Hon. Member.
I have been in discussion with many of the egg producers on this particular problem. 1 have suggested to the Minister of Agriculture that perhaps the feed component should be isolated as one of the variables which cannot be adhered to under the six and five program. However, the rest of the components of the cost of production formula, such as pullet cost, labour and so on, could be adhered to very easily. With that one exception, I believe the egg producer could continue under the
Supply
six and five program and show the same responsible pricing methods as they have in past years.

Mr. Speaker, when he has reached the end of his income and the bills are still not paid, the producer is in a pretty tough spot. There is no easy way out for him. There is no use saying he wants to co-operate. He does want to co-operate. It simply means he is going to go into bankruptcy. When he loses 4 cents or 5 cents on every dozen eggs he sells, it just means he is going to go that much deeper into debt until he just cannot continue to operate.
I have forwarded letters to both the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) and the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) in connection with this problem. If the policy of this Government is to keep agriculture viable, it has to take a realistic look at these things. If these egg producers go down the drain, what it will mean is that the larger corporations will take over and prices will go up for the consumers. There are no two ways about it: the consumer will have to pay more. I am trying to keep the price viable for the consumer by being reasonable with the egg producers today. I believe this is a responsibility which the Government should undertake, look at and resolve, not become part of the problem, but become, for a change, part of the solution.
This is a simple problem, it cannot be that hard to solve. If we do not, it means that the people of this country are going to pay more for their eggs or else go without them. The egg producer cannot continue to lose money on every dozen eggs he sells and stay in business. It is just that simple.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to respond to that. I am well aware of the margin of profit the egg producer has. The average for Canada is, I believe, 2.7 cents a dozen. I am confident that if the Minister of Agriculture follows the advice I gave him, and he indicated this morning that Cabinet was considering it and maybe even has made a decision, I think the problems of the egg producer will be resolved. I only hope the cattle producers would follow through with a similar plan so they could have the same level of stability.
Given all the problems I had as a Member of Parliament concerning farmers in financial difficulty in the last three and one half years, I have not had one egg producer, one dairy producer, one chicken broiler or turkey producer among them. So I think we have to recognize the importance of the cost of production formulas, that they have stood up to the challenge, and consequently I am confident that the Minister of Agriculture will use his persuasive powers to clear up any misunderstanding and that in the very near future we will have something to announce that will be acceptable to everyone.

Mr. Speaker, today's debate has centered on condemning the Government for its failure to recognize the economic hardship affecting all farmers in Canada, and its failure to alleviate that hardship by implementing good agricultural policies. The Minister said it was not really that much of a problem. According to his

October 21, 1983
Supply
Department's figures, 50 per cent of farmers have no debt. He said 35 per cent of the farmers in Canada own more than 85 per cent of their assets, so less than 15 per cent of their assets are in the form of debt. But he did admit that 5 per cent to 15 per cent are in financial difficulty, to use his term.
I think, Mr. Speaker, the hardship is more deeply ingrained than that and goes much beyond what the Minister has told to us today. I would like to spend a few moments outlining the situation as I see it. It seems to me the place to start is first to consider the realized net farm income, the costs farmers are subject to, and then to determine whether they are as a group able to move forward under that regime. I would then look at the debt statistics and the rate of debt increase, which I think will substantiate the allegations made by the Hon. Member for Portage-Marquette (Mr. Mayer) when he said there is extreme hardship out there on the farms and in agriculture.
Realized net income has been relatively stable. In 1974 it was $3.5 billion or $3.6 billion. In 1983 it was $3.7 billion. For over a decade farmers have had virtually the same net income, the one exception being in 1981 when they broke the $4 billion mark at $4.1 billion. But in 1980 it was down to $3.3 billion. However, it has been running along at $3.6 billion, or $3.5 billion. This in spite of the fact that costs in that period of time for all Canadians, and we are talking only about net farm incomes so we are talking about the take-home pay of the farm community, rose by well over 200 per cent, to be exact, 240 per cent. Just to bring us up to date, in the last four or five years we find the farm input price index has increased 29 per cent. That is between 1979 and 1983. At the same time farm commodity prices have increased only 11 per cent, with a resulting net income increase over those four years of 5 per cent. If you were to translate that into real dollars, it means a net decline in income of 25 per cent. So there has been in effect 25 per cent less spending power in the hands of Canadian farmers between 1979 and 1983. That leads us to conclude there is a very real possibility that hardship will occur.
Let us look at another set of data, that of the Farm Credit Corporation. Let us look at how many accounts are in arrears with the FCC as of September 30, 1983. Of beef producers with outstanding loans, 24 per cent are in arrears. Of crop producers with outstanding loans, 21 per cent are in arrears. That compares with a couple of years ago when only 14 per cent of the beef producers were in arrears, and only 14 per cent of crop producers were in arrears in 1981. If these people are not having financial difficulty, why are they so far in arrears? Why is the number of people in arrears going up? We have heard an argument, which seems to make some sense, that if farmers had marketing programs, they would not have those financial difficulties. I submit, Mr. Speaker, that the figures show that is no longer the case. Of farmers who were in fluid dairy production in 1981, only 6 per cent were in arrears with the FCC. However, as of September of this year 9.1 per cent were in arrears. That is the cream of the crop. That is the sector of the agriculture industry which is the best organized in terms of controlling production and also the most subsidized of any segment of agriculture. The amount of money in arrears
has increased 50 per cent in just two years. Producers are beginning to feel the pinch as well.
What about people in the poultry business? They are operating under supply management boards, and you would not think there would be many people in arrears with the FCC in that sector of agriculture. Yet we find that while in 1981 some 9.4 per cent were in arrears, today 14 per cent of them are in arrears on their FCC loans. In 1981, almost 21 per cent of hog producers were in arrears with their Farm Credit Corporation loans, and the same situation exists today.
Therefore, I believe that the allegation that there is hardship on the farms is correct. I am not sure that the immediate answer is simply to increase the amount of credit available. These people to whom I have been referring have had credit offered to them and they have had difficulty making their payments even on a 20-year or 30-year repayment schedule. The problem is not just one of needing more credit. The outstanding credit in Canadian agriculture was approximately $19 billion at the end of 1981. That figure is presently estimated to be $6 billion to $10 billion higher. The interest charges are now at the point where they are almost equivalent to the net farm income that farmers receive.
When I was attempting to begin farming about 25 years ago, there was a rule of thumb that one's sales from farming should be at least equivalent to one-fifth of the money invested in the farm. Much of the invested money would be borrowed, but that is beside the point. The theory was that one should be able to turn over the value of the farm once every five years so that the five-year sales should be at least equivalent to what was invested in the farm.
That is virtually impossible to achieve today in a cropping program, whether in western Canada or central Canada. In fact, a farmer who can turn over his assets in sales by ten years is doing extremely well. This means that the proportion of money that remains to the farmer to spend on his family, on reinvestment and improvements to his farm is shrinking all the time.
When I was deciding to become a farmer in the 1950s, farm economists and Government people were saying that there were obviously too many people involved in farming. They arrived at that conclusion then by taking the amount of income that is left, deciding what a good average wage would be and dividing that into the amount of income. In this way they concluded that there should be half as many farmers. With today's agricultural technology, I submit that it is quite difficult to argue that there are too many farmers. Today's farmers are very well equipped. They are using the latest technology and the latest information. They are working very long and hard hours. Even the academics are not making a case that there are too many farmers. They are not making the same arguments about under employment as were made in the 1950s and 1960s.
In fact, today's farmers face great financial hardship. I believe it is time to begin looking at some of the sources of that
October 21, 1983

hardship. We know that the most logical solution, one which many industrialized countries are in fact following, is to attempt to become as self-sufficient as possible in the production of food so that we do not have to rely on offshore producers for our livelihood. We discovered that in our country as a result of our experiments in dairy policy some 12 to 15 years ago. We decided to import some butter, cut back production and rely on those imports because it was much cheaper than it could be produced in our northern climate. When we finally arrived at an import position, our extra demand forced the world price of butter up so high that we could not afford to import it. We then moved to the program of subsidies and controlled production that is in place now. I suggest that is a reasonable policy for a country like ours, as it is for virtually any country.
However, we have not used that type of analysis in determining our needs for other products such as fruits and vegetables. If we were to extract our exports of grains from the import-export figures, there would actually be a net import requirement of approximately $2 billion in food products. These products are primarily fruits and vegetables. Even during the last 15 years our country has been processing fewer fruits and vegetables and has not been taking advantage of the very seasonal nature of our northern climate to keep them for the other eight to ten months that we are incapable of production because of the weather. We have given up those techniques to a large extent, with the result that farmers have had to ease out of producing some fruits and vegetables.
Let me point out some areas of the country where this is occurring. British Columbia is a traditional area of apple production in our country. The cost of production is estimated to be 14 cents per pound. Farmers receive approximately 4.5 cents at the farm, and there is a stabilization program in B.C. which adds another 2.5 cents. This means a seven-cent return to the farmer for a 14-cent outlay.
This situation does not only apply to British Columbia. With respect to the beef industry on the Prairies, the market yields approximately two-thirds of the actual cost of producing a pound of beef or pork.
In regard to potato production in the Maritimes, 50 per cent to 60 per cent of the costs are realized from the market while the rest adds to the debt of those particular farmers and increases the overburdening debt load that many of them face. This is causing a tremendous hardship.
The only solution is to do two and possibly three things. In the short term we have to devise better ways of providing short-term credit. More important, we must take action to solve the problem on a longer term basis. We must recognize that there should be some stabilization programs that are addressed at maintaining incomes by using costs rather than traditional market prices as the base. It makes no sense at all to have the historic market price as the base for stabilization programs.
In the British Columbia apple situation, the market is yielding only about a third of the costs. This has been the situation over the last three years. Even when the data base is
Supply
shortened to three years, it still means that the farmer will be stabilized at approximately 35 per cent to 50 per cent of his real production costs. Therefore that kind of stabilization program does not provide any stability to the farming sector or solve the problem of ever increasing debt.
Some Provinces have begun to develop programs based on costs, but this is done to a very limited extent since their financing capability is limited. They are also limited by the fact that much of the production goes beyond the Province, which means that any subsidy is essentially a subsidy to people who live outside the Province. We need a national stabilization program based on costs. Furthermore, we have to work hard at developing better marketing methods for those products, because there is no sense to having a stabilization program for a product that is not properly marketed. The buyers could take the attitude that they will pay a lower price because the farmer will take a very poor price for his product. The stabilization plan will simply go up to cover that price since it is cost based anyway. There should be a system of marketing the product linked to that stabilization program so that maximum returns can be gained from the market. We are seeing some experiments in that field in some Provinces. I note the beef programs in Manitoba and Saskatchewan and the hog programs in Ontario, Alberta, Saskatchewan, Manitoba and Prince Edward Island. They have been experimenting with that concept and it is one that is working relatively well.
I think it is generally agreed that a tripartite program involving the producer, his provincial Government and the federal level could provide an even better kind of program. Hopefully, the Government would be able to move very quickly on that kind of program, provided that some proposed legislation is introduced in the session, which, we are told, is imminent.
Finally, on the very short term, improved ways of permitting the turnover of land from one generation to the next is vital. We should be looking at reductions in the requirements for capital gains. We had that argument advanced several weeks ago in this House. Some new methods of transferring land from one generation to the other have been experimented with in some parts of the country with relatively good results.
The land bank in Saskatchewan allowed families who did not have a great deal of money to trade the land from one generation to the next and permitted them to roll it over to the following generation. This allows for relatively low cost production because the land does not have to be refinanced with each new generation and ultimately allows our country to compete effectively with those countries where land stays within the same family and is simply transferred from one generation to the next, free of charge. That is the system they have in certain parts of Europe. It is traditional. It allows us to compete effectively with producers whose land costs them practically nothing.
I close by urging the Government to reassess its agricultural program, to admit that hardship is being effected on producers

and that we move as quickly as possible to better marketing programs, stabilization programs and refinancing programs to overcome these problems.

Mr. Speaker, I have a couple of questions for the Hon. Member. He talks about the terrible plight farmers are in. He gives the impression that it is the case for all farmers. Is the Hon. Member aware that even in his Province land values have hardly decreased at all? Is he aware that the repayment ability of farmers in that province is the best in all of Canada? Is he aware that the Royal Bank is opening 12 or 14 new branches this year in Saskatchewan?

Yes, Mr. Speaker, I am aware that lending institutions are still very interested in Saskatchewan. I think that if you analyse the situation you will find that Saskatchewan was one of the last provinces to respond to the current difficulties by reducing the value of land. There are two reasons that land prices have not gone down in Saskatchewan as quickly as in other areas.
Because a Conservative Government was elected.

First, there was a fairly good crop for the last two years and the volumes moved have been fairly good. The Hon. Member beside me says it was a good Conservative Government that was elected. To some extent that has contributed. The Government has added not only to the 4 per cent reduction in the interest that is available for four years under the FCC, but it has extended that to any person looking for land who is under a certain age. That subsidy, though it is only short-term and will only apply for four years, has served to maintain the price of land. Therefore, rather than falling as dramatically as has been the case in some parts of Canada, the reduction in land prices is probably still to come in Saskatchewan.

Mr. Speaker, I just want to clarify that land prices have hardly gone down. With the increase in price of commodities, will the Hon. Member not agree they will probably go back up again? Canola seed oil is up $90 a tonne; canola oil meal is up $42; canola seed is up $40 a tonne, all in the space of about six weeks. That is more than enough to pay amply the increasing Crow rates for ten years. This has an effect, Mr. Speaker. Maybe the price of land going down in Saskatchewan has some effect. Would he not consider the question that Saskatchewan is overgoverned by 31 Cabinet Ministers for a population of less than one million people? Does the Hon. Member not think it is costly to run the crop insurance to which federally we contribute $56 million and to which producers contribute the other $56 million, while the Province spends $3 million or $4 million administering the program and has a special Cabinet Minister for it? Is that not a costly thing for farmers?

Mr. Speaker, there are a number of questions asked by the Minister. I will take the last one first. Yes, there has been a tremendous increase in the size of the Cabinet and
the cost of governing the Province. That has been reflected in the very large deficit in the order of $500 million to $600 million, a deficit which had not existed before. To some extent, I suppose, putting residents of the Province in debt into the future is perhaps being used to hold up some of the jobs in that Province.
With regard to the sudden increase in the price of canola, I would simply remind the House that the sudden surge in prices is very similar to the surge in prices we had in 1973 or 1974. It was very short-lived then and it will probably be short-lived now. We have not seen quite the same price levels for canola as we saw in 1974. Costs are something like 2.4 times as high now as then. Even with the sudden surge in prices, I do not think you will see a huge rush by Saskatchewan farmers to go out and start purchasing things.

Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the Hon. Member for Humboldt-Lake Centre (Mr. Althouse). Comparing the land bank program to the family farm purchase program, which is presently in place in Saskatchewan, up to the present time over 1600 individual family farm purchases have been assisted by the family farm purchase program. I would draw to the attention of the Chair that this is more than the whole land bank system had helped in the previous seven years. If the Hon. Member is serious, I would like to ask his opinion on the federal Government's refusal to accept some $200 million through the Province of Saskatchewan to the Farm Credit Corporation to be lent out to people in Saskatchewan to allow them to continue the family farm purchase program.
It was discriminatory and the human rights people would have been after us.
Oh, oh!

Mr. Speaker, one of the problems that exists with these kinds of programs is that the federal Government will have to decide when it cuts people off and when it does not. We have not had any reasons, and I do not know the reasons, for the federal Government having refused to accept a loan of $200 million, if indeed that loan was offered. The increase in purchases is in very large part due to this sudden availability of the 4 per cent reduction in interest. With the size of loans these days, that is pretty well enough to keep a family operating for a year. That 4 per cent reduction supplies them with food, clothing and automobiles. It would, of course, bring about a great many potential customers.
The problem with the program is that it is dependent upon the borrower being eligible under the rules of the FCC, which means that they have to have a fair amount of assets to begin with. People who would have qualified for the land bank program to get land do not often have those kinds of assets and therefore are not part of this program. There is some inequity as a result.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to rise to participate in this debate. There has been much misconception by Hon. Members opposite, which is evident in the motion itself. The entire state of the agricultural industry in Canada is not as the hon. proposer of the motion indicated.
I would like to cite a few statistics. Net farm income in Canada in 1983 will be up about 5 per cent above 1982 levels. The total cost of production to farmers at the same time will decline by about 3 per cent. Wheat is another example. Exports totalled 21.4 million tonnes, or three million tonnes more than in 1981-82. Grains and oilseed exports are up to 29.7 million tonnes. Barley is up approximately seven million tonnes, despite the fact that there have been tremendous surpluses of coarse grains in the United States. The price of canola to producers and western farmers is up about 20 per cent. If we look at pork, one of the difficult industries and one of the areas on which we should focus attention, in 1982-83 exports were 25 per cent to 30 per cent above 1981 levels. In the area of milk, through a system of supply management in Canada we have been able to keep our surpluses at a reasonable and manageable level. The contrary has occurred in the United States. It has incredible surpluses, about 12 per cent above requirements. The problems the Americans are facing in dealing with these surpluses are mindboggling.
The problem is not right across the board in agriculture. We must be responsible in pinpointing areas of concern and targeting on farmers who need help. As we all know, this is in the red meat area. Contrary to what is implicit in the motion before the House, our farmers are the most efficient of agricultural producers in all countries of the world, not only in terms of productivity but in terms of the quality of the products produced for consumption here and outside Canada. This enviable record is achieved despite the fact that 55 per cent of our agricultural lands are the most northerly of those of all other countries. Despite these hostile environmental factors, Canadian farmers are the most efficient producers of any in the world.
This has brought tremendous benefits, particularly for consumers. The cost of food to Canadian consumers is less than 16 per cent of their income. If this is not the best, it is the next to best record of any country. In addition, the efficiency and productivity of the farming community have led to reduced inflation in Canada. Our agricultural producers have to take a tremendous amount of the credit for the fact that our inflation rates are at a low level. In the statistics presented last week, the inflation rate was down to 5 per cent. Let us not forget the tremendous contribution to the Consumer Price Index and the
Supply
lowering of the rate of inflation by our agricultural community.
In focusing on what we might do to help farmers, let us recall that it is an area of divided jurisdiction. Under the Constitution, agricultural production is part federal and part provincial. Let us concentrate on some of the things the federal Government has undertaken. One problem mentioned has been the high cost of carrying credit or raising money to certain farmers. The federal Government has in place six programs designed to aid this situation-the Farm Credit Act, the Farm Credit Corporation Special Farm Assistance Program, the Farm Syndicates Credit Act, the Farm Improvement Loans Act, the Fruit and Vegetable Storage Construction Financial Assistance Program and the Small Business Bond Program.
By contrast I turn to the programs of the Province of Ontario, its four small, paltry programs. If the Ontario Minister of Agriculture thinks he can pass the buck to us for the farmers of my Province, he has another guess coming. He has not fulfilled his responsibilities to farmers in the area of credit assistance.
Turning to the red meat area, admittedly that is where there are the most problems. Almost all farm insolvencies relate to areas where there has not been some type of supply management program or marketing board program. The Ontario Minister of Agriculture proposed a stabilization program for red meat-producers, the Province and the federal Government each contributing a third. One would have to ask that Ontario Minister what happened to the program which was in effect in Ontario in the 1970s. It was a stabilization program that was similar in nature. It lasted a total of three years and fell flat on its face in the fourth year when only 10 per cent of farmers would contribute their third of the stabilization because prices went up and they would not need it that year. Is that any way to run the stabilization program? Is that the type of program that will provide security to producers who need it most in the circumstances?
This issue is fraught with politics. I realize the agricultural community is divided on the issue, but this does not mean that we should not attempt to follow the directions our experiences have indicated will work and have worked in the past. I welcome the leadership shown in this very vital area by our outstanding, knowledgeable and competent Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan).
Having looked at the present problem and having commented upon it, I feel we should also be looking forward and looking at what we as a federal Government might do on behalf of all Canadians to try to bring about greater equity and greater possibility for stable production and to try to help our farmers and ourselves.
I have five points upon which I would like to touch briefly. The first is the transportation system. In fact, the efficiency of production of western farmers or grain producers and their incredible productivity has been a mixed blessing. We can no longer envisage our present rail system being able to carry their grain to market under the present rate structure, if they continue producing at increased levels. The farmer's produc-

Supply
tivity has in fact brought upon us the need to rebuild our rail system to ensure that we have the capacity to export those products to market.
What are we doing today in this area? We have a Elouse which is not prepared to deal with that issue and debate it firmly. The best thing we can do for our western farmers is to ensure for them a rail capacity which will guarantee them exports. As a country and a nation we will be able to enter into export contracts with foreign purchasers, never having to fear the possibility that that grain cannot be taken to market.
With a new transportation system in the West, new port facilities, double-tracking, upgraded facilities and more cars, we will be able to assure our foreign buyers that our product can be delivered to them on time. This is critical to the prairie farmer as well. He would not have to worry about the export logjam. He can go ahead producing his product, his wheat, with the assurance that we can do the job of exporting it. It will cost him less to store the crops on his land. He will have better cash flow.
The single one thing that will do more for the western farmer than anything else, apart from higher world prices, is the ability of Canadians to compete more effectively in the export markets through an increased rail capacity. That is why essential to what we are doing in our transportation program today is to increase the capacity of our rail system to carry the western farmers' product to market.
The second area I would like to touch upon briefly is the whole field of research and development. Why are we among the most efficient producers of agricultural products in the world? It is because we have undertaken tremendous research and development in order to produce new crops, plants and types of cattle and beef that stand up to Canadian climate and conditions and which can be exported. Marquis wheat is one example, canola is another. We have 72 different nations sending their agricultural representatives to Canada to find out how we are doing some of these things.
Look at the entrepreneurial flare of many Canadians and what they have been able to do. E. P. Taylor has put Canada on the international map in terms of the types of bloodstock he has been able to produce. There are many Canadians who have followed in his footsteps. One of them I know very well. Anderson Farms, which started out ten years ago near St. Thomas, is now a leading exporter of stock to the United States and elsewhere. We have seen what the Holstein cow, developed in Canada, has done for milk production in many other countries. We are now advancing our technology of open transplants and exporting semen. We are able to bring these technologies, these new ways of doing things, to many other nations of the world. This is critical to what we are doing.
Agriculture Canada spends more than $200 million a year on this type of research and development. It goes into soils, plants, water, energy, equipment, animals, food processing, all these types of areas. We have produced 30 to 40 new plant varieties for the benefit of Canadian farmers in the grains,
fruits and vegetables areas. After Agriculture Canada was able to find these products, rather than keeping them to itself, it has put them out through the SeCan Association for immediate distribution to the farmers so that the benefits of these new technologies become immediately available. SeCan is presently handling 77 new varieties of plants.
I am very proud of the research and development record in Canada. However, this record does not mean we can sit pat. Our competitors abroad are getting more deeply into these areas as well. It is our obligation to devote more and more effort to high-level research and development in Canada.
A short while ago 1 had the pleasure of visiting Red Williams in Saskatoon and seeing his tremendous research facilities, of which he is very proud. That Canadian has achieved an international reputation. We need more of this type of individual in our agricultural research in Canada.
The third area we should be looking at in terms of agricultural policy is the whole concept of foreign aid. Except in emergency-like situations such as floods or extreme drought, I do not believe that exporting surplus Canadian food to developing countries is the answer to either their problem or our need for foreign markets. It is critical that they have this food when people are starving. I am not denigrating that role for food aid at all. Even more important than food aid over the longer term is bringing these new agricultural technologies to the developing countries. Our role as a leader in research and development, biotechnologies and the new techniques, as a nation that has developed many new types of animals, plants and trees which can stand up to the harsh vigours of the Canadian environment, gives us a tremendous role to play in exporting those agricultural technologies to the Third World countries. The greatest thing we can do for those nations is to make them self-sufficient in food. They would not have to spend their very scarce foreign exchange reserves on importing produce from other nations. They would be able to feed their people through cycles of drought, heat or pestilence with new products that we with our expertise can help them develop. I believe this would be the greatest contribution we could make in the name of humanity.
A fourth area to look at where we should explore further possibilities to assist the agriculture community and all Canadians is in the area of taxation. I welcome the provisions of the April 19 budget in which the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) extended loss carryovers so that those farmers who have experienced difficulty over the past couple of years will be able to spread those losses backwards and forwards to a far greater extent so that income taxes payable before or in the future can be offset by those losses. The farmers will have the cash.
Very important, and some Members have mentioned it today, is the issue of capital gains. In many instances, the farm is the retirement security for the farmer. If the children do not want to take it over and benefit from the capital gains rollover, if they do not have children who can take it over, if they are forced or want to leave the farm because of age or illness, we have to look very seriously at whether we should be taking the
October 21, 1983

slice of taxes that we are out of that retirement security, namely the farm, which they worked so hard to build up and into which they have put so much. I am very partial to recommendations to take a second look at changing the valuation day to 1974 and offering farmers the option of either choosing 1972 or 1974 as a valuation year for valuing their farms and disposition. 1 think we should also look very carefully at the impact that inflation might have had upon the value of their farms, and I think we should ask ourselves if it is right, if it is proper and if it is the most efficient use of resources to tax farmers on inflationary gains from that valuation year of 1972 or 1974.
The fifth area I would like to touch upon very briefly in the one minute left to me is the whole concept of self-sufficiency. We have within our means the ability to produce more foodstuffs in Canada. The consumers of Canada will benefit and they can help us by buying Canadian goods, even if they are buying Canadian fruits that are canned. Why do we always need to have fresh fruit throughout the winter? Why do we have to import fruit? Why could we not be growing more of our own foodstuffs in greenhouses, which would take advantage of the tremendous energy surpluses, particularly of western gas? There are tremendously imaginative new methods from which, if implemented, we can all benefit.
The agriculture industry is not the disaster that the Hon. Members opposite have indicated. It is one of the most dynamic, forward looking, entrepreneurial industries in the country. It is one of the best. We should all be proud of what the agriculture industry and the farmers have been able to achieve.

Mr. Speaker, since I come from eastern Ontario and represent what is primarily a rural constituency, I welcome the opportunity to discuss agriculture and its importance to Canada. I have always admired the forthrightness, foresight and determination of Canadian farmers. They have had the ability to lead by example, to thrive on challenge and to increase the efficiency which has built the country. Agriculture helped to build the country with roots which are deep and strong. Determination, sharing and hard work have helped to overcome adversaries in all shapes and forms. Our tradition is strong and we are slow to change from the known to the unknown simply for the sake of change alone.
The federal Government should follow the lead of the farmers with the many attributes which have been ascribed to them, which include those of leadership, self-sufficiency, unity and hard work. These qualities will help in bringing about solutions to the very real problems facing Canadian farmers today.
One problem facing Canadians is that of energy. We all use various forms of energy, and farmers are no exception. Rising
Supply
fuel costs and security of supply are important matters that must be faced in the near future.
We are fortunate here in Canada to have the potential for energy self-sufficiency. The Government's energy policy proclaims self-sufficiency by the year 1990. However, what we see as a result of its policies are uncertainty, increased costs and indecisiveness all across the country.
Farmers have not only been plagued by high energy costs, but because of the federal Government's interests rate policy, they have also been hit with high financing costs. As a result of high financing costs, many independent farmers have been forced into bankruptcy. Economic hardship in the agricultural sector can have a far-reaching impact affecting the welfare of many people other than farmers and their families.
We have observed the extension of such problems into the farm machinery industry and other farm supply industries as farmers have been forced to curtail expenditures and new capital investment. The need for new capital investment in the farming community continues even though many farmers cannot afford to borrow. Machinery continues to wear out and must be replaced, but it is expensive. If money is put into machinery, it is not used to put food on the table of the farmer. Every day the need for adequate funding for the Farm Credit Corporation grows. Daily financial pressures are forcing farmers to go to the Farm Credit Corporation and farmers are increasingly being told: "Sorry, there is no money".
The Farm Credit Corporation recently requested permission to borrow $600 million from foreign money markets in order to finance the corporation until March, 1984. Finance Department officials turned a deaf ear to this request. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde), when questioned in the House of Commons, stated that $250 million was adequate. The Minister's response only goes to show his lack of understanding of the problems facing Canada's farming community.
Another problem facing the farming community is that of retirement. The nature of the agricultural industry and the present tax system create many problems that other industries do not face. Incomes tend to be very erratic, fluctuating with the extremes of weather, the changes in domestic and foreign commodity markets and general economic conditions as a whole. A large percentage of any profit made by a farmer goes directly back into the farm in order to finance the purchase of additional land, cattle, fertilizer, machinery and the like.
At present, farmers have no over-all pension fund other than the Canada Pension Plan. Because the farmer's income is so erratic, his ability to contribute to an RRSP is greatly reduced. There is an old saying that goes: "Farmers are cash poor but asset rich". However, that saying does not answer the question of where a farmer will get a pension when he or she becomes unable to farm in later life. Historically, the farmer's pension has been his farm.
The proceeds of the sale of a farm are eligible for capital gains tax. In the November 12, 1981, federal budget, the IAAC was replaced by forward averaging. This has caused a
