great deal of concern because of the potential long-run divergence between interest and inflation rates.
I believe, Mr. Speaker, that the Minister of Finance should re-examine his policy of levying capital gains taxes upon farmers and their farms and that he should also review his forward averaging policies in order to allay the fears expressed by the farming community.
Having heard that the Province of Ontario proposes to introduce agriculture as a compulsory part of the core science courses in grades seven through ten, I strongly urge the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) to support this provincial initiative and to urge other Provinces to follow suit. Such courses would make the job of Minister of Agriculture much easier.
To many people, and in particular the Minister of Finance, are unaware of the importance of agriculture to the Canadian economy. Agriculture accounts for one-sixth of all economic activity in Canada. The agricultural sector employs 18 per cent of the Canadian work force and generates nearly 12 per cent of Canada's exports. However, the recession has hit hard. Farm bankruptcies have soared to record numbers, and one agricultural economist has estimated that the recession has taken $5.5 billion worth of assets off the national farm balance sheet.
The Progressive Conservative Party has announced a ten-point program to help the producers survive this recession. We called for greater funding to the Farm Credit Corporation. The Minister of Agriculture agreed with us but his colleague, the Minister of Finance, ignored his advice and slashed the Farm Credit Corporation's request for more funds by over 55 per cent. We called for the establishment of an agri-bond program. The Minister of Agriculture agreed, but again the Minister of Finance has refused to implement such a program.
We called for an improved stabilization plan. Once again, the Minister of Agriculture agreed. However, the Minister of Finance did not agree and, as a result, Canadian producers will continue to suffer from a plan that does not fully take into account rising production costs and a plan that makes its payments after much of the economic damage has been done. We called for revisions to the capital gains tax and other taxation matters. Again, the Minister of Agriculture agreed with the need for such revisions, but again the Minister of Finance has refused to make any changes, although his predecessor did consider a study of the matter.
It is clear from this list that the Minister of Finance is not aware of the importance of and opportunities in Canadian agriculture, nor is he aware of the problems besetting this vital Canadian resource. With the establishment of compulsory agricultural courses at the secondary school level, hopefully future Ministers of Finance will not suffer from the same ignorance.
Recent figures on Farm Credit Corporation loan approvals point to a poor credit picture for financially troubled or beginning farmers seeking mortgages from the federal lending
agency. In July, the FCC got approval to borrow $250 million more. It needed at least $600 million. This $250 million just will not cover the tremendous need and demand from farmers.
This is a real danger if we continue on our present course. In 1981, there were 318,361 census farms in Canada, a 12 per cent decline from 366,128 of 1971, and a 57 per cent decline from the 732,858 of 1941. We all know that farms are larger and more efficient but we also know there is a limit to efficiency, and now we see the numbers of farms going out of production at an alarming rate. In the 40 years between 1941 and 1981 the farm population in Canada decreased by nearly 66 per cent, a rate of decline averaging some 4,300 persons per month. Atlantic Canada has suffered the worst with farm population declines of approximately 93 per cent in both New Brunswick and Nova Scotia. Farmers are our unsung heroes. In 1940 the average Canadian farm produced enough food to feed 11 people; today an average farm feeds over 60 people. This trend has reached a peak because of the lack of reward for the hard work which is associated with farming.
The net farm income as a proportion of gross farm income has slumped from 37 per cent in 1965 to 19.6 per cent in 1982. In 1965, gross farm income was $4 billion and net farm income was $1.5 billion. In 1970, gross farm income was $4.4 billion and net farm income was $1.3 billion, or 28.8 per cent. In 1982, gross farm income was $19.3 billion and farm income was $3.8 billion.
Agriculture Canada has estimated that production costs will increase by 11 per cent in 1981 and 1986. Farm operating expenses increased 115 per cent between 1976 and 1982. The Minister of Agriculture brags about cheap food and being able today to buy more eggs with a dollar than before. If this trend continues consumers will not be able to buy farm products at any price. What about costs of production and the prices of farm products which have not kept pace? Mr. Speaker, one factor alone which the Government has placed on the backs of our farmers is the costs which stem from the deficit and indirect costs of energy and the federal farm fuel tax which accounts for one quarter of farm operating expenses. In 1972, interest charges comprised 8.6 per cent of farm operating expenses. In 1982, this has grown to 13.9 per cent of farm operating expenses.
It is a crime that FCC does not have the funds available. Farmers in Ontario given conditional loan approvals last summer will have to wait until at least 1984 for any hope of getting these funds.
Settlement in Hastings-Frontenac-Lennox and Addington on June 16, 1784 by United Empire Loyalists was a situation of which we have little understanding today. These settlers, who faced starvation, planted turnips that summer and survived on rations of food until the first crop could be grown the next year. From this hearty stock of first farmers in Ontario came future generations of farmers who, to this very day, owe so much to their ancestors. 1984 will mark this bicentennial of agriculture in Ontario, and I hope the Minister of Agriculture will make every effort to recognize this significant contribution to the history of agriculture in Canada during 1984.
October 21, 1983

There is a vital role for Governments to play in agriculture such as the promotion of soil conservation, the safeguarding and managing of water resources, agricultural research and the conserving of genetic resources. However, Government intervention frequently goes far beyond such concerns since it is often motivated by political consideration and a very narrow view of economic gain.
In a recent report by the science and technology division of the Library of Parliament on world food security it was stated that not so many years ago, the promise of the green revolution seemed to have calmed down fears about society's ability to feed a burgeoning world population. Agricultural technology held the prospect of pushing the problem of food supply far into the future. Between 1950 and 1971, world grain production almost doubled, and despite a rate of population increase unmatched in human history, per capita grain production rose by more than 30 per cent. Today, agricultural systems in developed and developing countries alike are experiencing difficulties, although the causes vary.
The question that arises from this statement is whether or not central planning, uneconomic price ceilings, import restrictions, export taxes, and subsidies established by the Government of Canada have created the problem of supply and distribution, not only affecting the market in Canada but also the world. Increasingly, Canadian agricultural policies are being felt throughout the world because of our large exports of agricultural produce. Canada is one of the largest exporters of grain in the world. What would happen to the world if Canada's grain farmers found that they would no longer afford to supply cheap grain to the hungry masses of people? The result would be that many hundreds of people would die. In light of this fact, the Canadian Government and people have an added responsibility to ensure that our farmers can meet such demands, at home as well as abroad.
Are there any questions or comments? There being no questions or comments, we will proceed to debate. The Hon. Member for Carleton-Char-lotte (Mr. McCain).

Early last year, the State of Maine launched an appeal to the U.S. Department of Commerce to declare that potatoes, round whites in particular, had been dumped into the United States and that they had damaged the return of the industry in the State of Maine and the eastern seaboard. This is very alarming to eastern Canada because we do rely upon shipping a portion of our crop on a near annual basis to the eastern seaboard of the United States. If that market is eliminated or if the return from that market is reduced, it will very seriously affect the income of the Atlantic farmer in the potato industry. However, that is not where it stops, Mr. Speaker. This is where I criticize other areas of Canada. If the export market to the United States reduces the net return to the farmer of Atlantic Canada, at the same time it reduces the net return to every potato producer east of Thunder Bay. Every potato producer in Quebec and Ontario will suffer because of an oversupply of potatoes which would ordinarily have been exported but must now be marketed in eastern Canada, east of Thunder Bay at its extremity. That is the consequence. Unfortunately, the hearings ended in a successful result of the application of the State of Maine, and on July 26 it was found by the Department of Commerce that:
We have preliminarily determined that there is a reasonable basis to believe or suspect that fall-harvested, round white potatoes from Canada are being, or are likely to be, sold in the United States at less than "fair value", as provided in Section 733 of the Tariff Act 1930, as amended (19 U.S.C. 1673) (the Act).

Minister Regan noted that officials have not yet had time to study the U.S. Commerce Department's preliminary determination in detail but would be doing so to ensure that the United States is acting in conformity with its international obligations.

The U.S. Government imposed am import penalty tax on potatoes from the Maritime Provinces today in an interim decision subject to review.

This imposes a virtual embargo on all except for those most gambling of individuals on this product imported into Canada. The ITC found in a split decision last March that there were preliminary indications of injury to U.S. producers.

complaint, if we allow this proposal to become law without a formal protest, we may well look forward to its extention to the feed, grain and oil seed industries, and goodness only knows what other industries.

Mr. Speaker, at this time last week I was in my riding and I had the pleasure of attending the sale ring of the local livestock co-op. They ran through about 1,500 hundred head that day, mostly of calves. Good steer calves were going for about 75 cents a pound. The last time I sold calves in that same sale ring was in 1973 and I got 73 cents a pound. 1 can remember at that time paying about 38 cents to 40 cents a gallon for gasoline, and you know what a gallon of gasoline is worth now.
What is it worth?

It is about $2.40, something like that. In any event, cattle receipts today are low, costs have probably tripled and people are in real trouble. Many farmers and ranchers have had to take jobs off the farm to try to meet their mortgage and operating expenses. This seems like a very normal thing to do because you are trying to save your business and stay afloat. All was well in my riding until about January this year when the Department of National Revenue sent in teams of auditors who decided that these ranchers, because they were making an off farm income, had to be recategorized from full-time farmers to part-time or even hobby farmers. What is worse, they went back as far as four years and are now sending out reassessments as high as $75,000 and literally bankrupting many of these people.
If you do not think this is a problem, Mr. Speaker, I can lay out the evidence to show you it really is. It is a problem right across the country. In 1981, Statistics Canada claimed that over 39 per cent of all farmers and over 50 per cent of beef farmers are working off the farms to the extent of 171 days a year. I know that in 1982, approximately 125,000 had off farm income. Yesterday I received a zerox copy of an advertisement for a herd dispersal sale involving 100 head of cattle. This is Kelso Angus in Georgetown, Ontario, and what is interesting about this is that at the bottom it says, "A victim of Section 31 of the Income Tax Act". Kelso Angus had been designated as a hobby farm under an interpretation of this Act and as a result of subsequent assessment they were left with no alternative but totally to disperse this major herd which was just attaining the peak of its young productive life. I say that is a disgrace and it should not be happening in this country, Mr. Speaker. 1 have literally a couple of hundred cases as bad as that. I am going to read from a few letters I have received because they set out the problem so succinctly that I think it will drive home to you how very serious the problem is.

The first letter is from a lady at 150 Mile House, British Columbia, who was audited in January and received a reassessment in April. In May she received a call from the auditor, a Mr. Wilson, stating that they would only be reassessed for 1981, not 1979 and 1980 as previously indicated. He did not give any reason. These people merely went about their business and purchased an old bailer and a pick-up truck thinking that they would have only one year's income tax bill to pay at the worst. Then, all of a sudden, the same auditor phoned back to say he made a mistake and these people would be reassessed for all three years. That just goes to show the incompetence of these auditors, Mr. Speaker. None of them have any agriculture expertise, and we have proved that already in this House.
1 have another letter from Quesnel, British Columbia. These people were audited on March 16 and were told they were now classified as a hobby farm because they had no reasonable expectation of a profit. They had three weeks in which to appeal, they went straight to their accountant, found they showed a profit this year and would be glad to show the auditor the books. So they met, and the auditor changed his mind a bit but said that he was still going to classify it as a hobby farm. They then sent their appeal letter, a copy of which came to me, on March 30, and on May 3 the auditor phoned and said he reviewed their case and they were now classified as part-time farmers. In other words, they could deduct up to $5,000, and was that okay with them? She said yes but that her husband was not home and she wanted to ask him before agreeing finally. She asked the auditor on the phone twice if this means they do not owe the Government anything and he said twice, "No, you don't. You don't owe us anything." The next day he phoned back and asked if she had talked to her husband and if he agreed with the decision. She said that he did. The auditor said that as long as he agrees, he did not have to send them a letter. She said no, that she would like the letter. He said that it would take a couple of weeks, and that was okay with her.
Two weeks went by without any letter. She phoned the auditor on May 30 and asked why she had not received her letter. He said that they had reviewed their appeal again and decided that they were back to being assessed as hobby farmers. She asked why she was not notified, and he replied that it had been in the works for "the last two weeks". That was the only reason he gave. She then asked again if they owed the Government anything, and he said yes, as far as his office was concerned.
How can people conduct their business when the tax department harasses them in that manner? Another fact which has come to light is that many young farmers are being hit under Section 31 of the Income Tax Act. I would like to read one case from the presentation that was put together by the Minister of Agriculture for Ontario. He composed a 22-page document called "Income Tax Treatment of Small and PartTime Farmers" which he presented this summer to the Interprovincial and Federal Provincial Conference of Ministers and the Deputy Ministers of Agriculture in Prince Edward Island.

It is an indictment of the whole problem that I am bringing to the attention of the House in regard to Section 31 of the Income Tax Act.
In this report he points out particularly how absolutely wretched this situation is as far as farmers starting out are concerned. I will just read the one case which he uses as an example:
In 1974, Mr. A bought a half-section of land for grain farming, the price of which was partially financed by a mortgage and partially by savings. He gradually added to the size of his farm, so that by 1979 he had 800 acres, and had also acquired a full line of farming machinery. Again, these additions were financed by savings and by outside borrowings. During this period, Mr. A had kept his job at a uranium mine, where he was employed on a seven-day-on-seven-days off shift basis.
Mr. A found that with the help of his wife and his two teenage sons, the seven consecutive days off every second week were enough to enable him to carry on his grain farming operation. He also took one week's vacation in the spring and one week in the fall which, together with his regular time off, allowed he and his family to do the planting and harvesting of the crops.
By 1980, Mr. A felt confident enough about the future of his farm that he gave up his job to devote his full time to the farming operation. Unfortunately, his timing was unlucky, and the combination of high interest rates, low grain prices, dry conditions, grasshopper infestation and higher general operating costs forced him to take another job in early 1981.
While this would seem to be an example of an individual genuinely trying to get a start in the farming business, and committing practically all of his capital and most of his energies to the business, Revenue Canada invoked Section 31 and limited Mr. A's farm loss deduction to $5,000 annually. Mr. A's objection to the Appeals Division of Revenue Canada has been rejected, and if he wishes to carry his case further, he must now go to either the Tax Review Board or the Federal Court, either one of which will be a costly and time-consuming procedure.
There are three other examples given here which are all as bad, if not worse.
An interesting thing which is mentioned here and in the other cases is the fact that the wives and children in all of these cases generally work many long hours on these farms, and this labour is not recognized at all by the Department of Revenue. If a farmer employs someone the Department will recognize that. While that is in the farmer's favour, the Department will not credit any labour by the wife or children.
As well, the Department states that if someone has a full-time job, that person does not have the time to spend on the farm. Luckily, the wife of a rancher in my riding kept a diary in 1980. The rancher had a job in a mill where he worked 37.5 hours a week. He put in a total of 1,950 hours that year. In the same year he put in 2,260 hours on his farm. This does not count the hours put in by his wife and children. Of course, the auditors coming from the city figure that if one puts in a 7.5-hour day, that is all one is good for. It only proves that they do not understand farming or what makes a farm or ranch work.
Since I first brought up this issue in the House approximately a year ago, I have managed to get the attention of the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan). He writes different replies on the subject to almost anyone who writes him a letter, but at least he is beginning to realize that there might be a problem.
I have copies of letters that he has written to people all across the country. They are interesting and I will read a few
key sentences. I have a letter dated May 31 which is a written to a Mr. Lyle Klein of Quesnel, British Columbia, in which he states: "I am in favour of a thoroughgoing review of Section 31 because this provision means that farming is treated differently than other businesses and that the full losses from other businesses can be deducted from the taxpayers' income from other sources."
The Minister says, in a letter to David Kirk, Executive Secretary of the Canadian Federation of Agriculture dated June 17, "Now is the time to address the basic issue of why there should be any limitation on loss deductibility for farming businesses when there is no such limitation in respect of other businesses the taxpayer may pursue." In the final paragraph, he says, "I personally regard Section 31 as a priority issue in agriculture at the present time."
I submit that one surely would not know that it is a priority with him if one tried to do some of the things I have done to get his attention.
In an August 8 letter to Mr. Brian Griffith, President of the Ontario Aberdeen-Angus Association, the Minister of Agriculture said, "My own view is similar to yours in that I am not comfortable with the $5,000 limitation under Section 31 on the deduction which can be made from other sources of income with respect to farming losses. If the person passes the test of having a genuine farming business, I would favour the unlimited loss deductibility which applies to non-agriculturai businesses." The Minister is finally realizing that there is a problem.
It did not take the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) as long. I received a reply from him to letters I had written to him on June 6. He said, "I am disturbed by the number of letters and press clippings that I have received illustrating that a rigid application of the restrictive farm loss rules can result in an unfair taxation of bona fide farmers." While he does not go on to say that he will do anything about it, he realizes that there is a problem.
The assessments in my riding are now pouring in. There are approximately 150 people who are getting their reassessment notices, and most of them are anywhere from $5,000 to $75,000. It is interesting to see what happens. The minute one receives that notice, the collection division of Revenue Canada immediately begins its attack. Generally, it phones to say that it demands the amount of money immediately, whether or not that person intends to appeal his case.
People should be aware of the fact that they do not have to pay cash. Some have been foolish enough to borrow money from the bank to pay, but it is possible to go to the bank and arrange for a letter of credit. It costs .5 per cent per year. That will keep the taxman away until the hearing is completed.
If that does not work, they can put a lien on the ranch or farm, and that is not advisable. What is interesting about the letter of credit is that if the case is lost, the bank has to forward that money immediately to the Department of Revenue. The bank then debits the account and makes it a demand loan. With a $100,000 operating loan, for example, the bank
October 21, 1983

would deduct that letter of credit from the total operating loan so that the person would be cut back during that interval.
When a person receives an assessment, there is an opportunity to file a notice of objection. Generally there is 90 days to file that objection. It will take approximately two to three months to hear from the Department of Revenue. It appears that the Department of Revenue is simply rubberstamping these objections and throwing them out without given them any consideration. I presume that the Department does not want to admit that anyone has made a mistake. When an objection is overruled, the next step is to go to the tax court of Canada. In order to do that, you have to write to Ottawa to the Court of Administration at 381 Kent Street, Ottawa and ask for an appointment. It might take up to two or three months or even longer to get an appointment with the tax court. You go before a judge. You do not need to have a lawyer. It does not cost you anything. It is probably a good idea though to have a lawyer. You go before the judge and, hopefully, if you win the case, you are all right. But if you do not, the only thing left is to go to the Supreme Court of Canada. You have to go through the court system, which is terribly expensive. I know of only one person with whom I have been in contact out of about 500 who is going that route.
There was an interesting case of a chap at 100 Mile House who has a horse farm. That throws taxation auditors into a tizzy. They do not understand horses at all. They do not understand cattle, goats or anything else as far as I am concerned, but horses really throw them for a loop. Tax people claim that horse breeding is not classed as a legitimate business in Canada. That is their stand on horse breeding. This particular chap was reassessed about $70,000. He went to the bank to try to get a letter of credit. Because he did not have a great line of operating credit, he did not get the amount needed. Revenue Canada is now forcing him to sell his horses. This will put him into receivership. At the same time he has launched an appeal. He wants to go to the tax court, but he will be broke long before he gets there.
This problem is damaging to agriculture. It removes the incentive for anyone wanting to get into farming. I had a person in my office last week. When he went through some of the stuff with me I found he had 500 acres of land, but he decided to let it sit there. As long as we have this kind of legislation and these kinds of over-zealous auditors and a Minister of Revenue who is as heartless as he appears to me to be, agriculture in Canada will go nowhere.

Mr. Speaker, I am happy to have this opportunity this afternoon to take part in a debate introduced by the Hon. Member for Portage-Marquette (Mr. Mayer). The Government has been accused in this resolution of not responding to the financial needs of farmers. It provides
Supply
us on this side with a very useful occasion to put a few facts on the record.
I come from an area that is no longer truly agricultural but I do have, in two or three of my municipalities, a substantial dairying industry. In another part of my constituency, the black earth area, I have a very fast growing industry in the production of vegetables, many of which are being exported to the United States in numbers and quantities that last year exceeded revenues of $16 million and this year will probably be in the order of at least $20 million. This is a small geographic area but it is an extremely rich agricultural area. Exports of vegetables are penetrating markets that have never been penetrated before by Canadian products. Markets are being penetrated largely because the federal Government has been helpful in many areas, either providing for refrigerated storage allowing, for example, carrots to be kept in perfect condition until late spring or early summer, even carried over from the previous year, or, in the case of some salad crops, providing assistance in fast chilling facilities.
The federal Government has been helpful and it is paying off for the Canadian economy. To accuse the present Minister of not doing his best for agriculture is really a travesty. I think every Canadian farmer knows that the present Minister has been a staunch defender of farmers' interests whenever he has had the opportunity in Cabinet to do that. I am sure in many, many a Cabinet meeting the present Minister has been an "enfant terrible" in favour of the interests of Canadian farmers, and his actions have paid off in a number of the new programs that we have seen.
[ Translation]
I would especially like to mention a few items concerning the dairy industry, which is an important sector in an area like the federal riding of Chateauguay. Canada's dairy industry has had to face two major setbacks in recent years. A drop in domestic demand for dairy products was followed by a spectacular drop in prices as result of reduced demand and an unprecedented surplus of over two million tons in other countries producing dairy products. We are now overcoming these problems thanks to our supply management program and other federal policy measures. The dairy program has been in effect since 1975, with changes being made regularly following recommendations and meetings with members of the dairy industry.
As far as subsidies are concerned, in order to maintain the importance of our dairy industry, subsidies are granted directly to producers of industrial milk. At the present time, the subsidy is $6.03 per hectoliter on shipments meeting domestic requirements. It is expected that $280 million in subsidies will be paid during the present dairy campaign which started August 1.
Last year, Quebec producers received $132 million in subsidies. Within the framework of our national dairy policy, the Federal Government determines a target price for processed milk and cream to ensure that increases in production costs of

October 21, 1983
Supply
dairy producers are covered by market prices. The target price is calculated according to a formula established in 1975, which allows for variations in production costs and other factors. The price serves as a guide for provincial milk marketing boards and in setting prices for processed milk and cream in the provinces. The present target price is $42.80 per hectoliter.
In 1975, when the present national dairy policy was established, the target price was set at $25. This means there has been an increase of 72 per cent. According to Mr. Garon, the Quebec Minister responsible for Agriculture, the Federal Government is doing nothing for farmers. However, we have increased income from industrial milk by 72 per cent since 1975.
Since 1975, Federal Government expenditures with respect to dairy products have averaged $300 million per year. These funds are helping to ensure the continued development of the Canadian dairy industry.

1 would like to mention one other area we tend to neglect when we talk about agriculture. A tremendous contribution has been made by our agricultural research. These policies have contributed not only to agriculture but to the Canadian economy by strengthening the quality of our agricultural products and thus our ability to compete in world markets.
We spend more than $200 million a year on agri-food research. This amounts to almost half of what is being spent by all organizations in the country, both private and public, on that kind of research. We have developed, as a result, one of the most successful and productive agricultural systems in the world. Plant breeding has gained for Canada a reputation second to none. A whole variety of new plants which are able to defeat diseases and increase yield have been developed. The Department produces 30 to 40 new plant varieties each year for the benefit of Canadian farmers. They cover a wide variety of crops, including grains, fruit and vegetables. Oilseeds have been a particular success story. Canola, rapeseed which was a Canadian research success story-
It was a bad word, and you know it.

Canola is now giving Canada about $500 million a year in foreign exchange. This is what it is worth from an export point of view. It is an extremely important product, not only for Canadian farmers but for the rest of the economy because of the secondary effects of that money. There has been a succession of new varieties of wheat over the years.
Something which is of particular interest to my part of the world, about which I might as well be talking, is this new Leger barley variety. It is now available for the first time to Canadian farmers. It outyields all other barleys grown in eastern Canada by wide margins. Leger barley is so promising that it could supplant all other barleys grown in Ontario, Quebec and the Atlantic Provinces over the next few years. It
could reduce the dependency of eastern farmers, particularly those in Quebec and the Maritimes, on grain for animal feed imported from outside their provincial borders. One day Leger barley could help make eastern Canada self-sufficient in grain grown for animal feed, along with new corn varieties which require an ever shorter growing season and which, combined, put a lie to the kind of propagandistic opposition of some farmers' organizations against changes to the Crow. In effect, this kind of argument was being made to stir up eastern farmers against the Crow arrangement. It was to the effect that they would be paying so much more for western grain that they would never be able to compete, etc. What nonsense! Within a few years eastern Canada will be self-sufficient in feed grain production. In my view that argument was totally false, as are many of the arguments used against the Crow in the West.

Finally, Mr. Speaker, I would like to mention, but only briefly, because I would like to let others ... I would like to mention the compensation plan for apple growers in Eastern Canada. In the winter of 1980-1981 and the following spring, severe frost caused very serious damage to orchards in Eastern Canada. In many cases, producers suffered losses of over 50 per cent. After a thorough analysis of the situation, the Federal Government, in consultation with apple growers in the areas concerned, developed a compensation and reestablishment plan. We want to help apple growers in Eastern Canada recover their full production capacity. The compensation provisions are as follows: between now and December 31, 1984, apple growers will receive compensation for trees damaged in 1980-1981. Forty dollars per standard tree will be paid to cover the cost of removal of dead trees and preparing the soil for new plantings. New plantings in the orchards concerned will be covered by the plan as follows: As soon as the orchards destroyed by frost have been replanted, $16 per standard tree will be paid to cover the cost of maintaining the new trees until they start producing.
Mr. Speaker, I feel this is a major contribution towards helping our apple growers, and an indication of the assistance the Government is giving to farmers across the country. I shall not comment any further, since 1 would like to give the Official Opposition a chance to finish the debate.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Any questions? Comments? Debate. The Hon. Member for Wetaskiwin (Mr. Schellenberger) has the floor.

Mr. Speaker, in the dying minutes of Friday afternoon it gives me pleasure to rise and conclude the debate. I was very pleased to hear the comments of the Hon. Member for Chateauguay (Mr. Watson). He expressed some very progressive thoughts on the Crow rate. I see the former Minister of Transport is present today. He probably listened with a very open mind to those
October 21, 1983

comments. He should have acted when he was Minister, and we would have had a lot fewer problems and difficulties in the whole Crow debate. They were very progressive thoughts, and I was pleased to hear them being expressed by the Hon. Member for Chateauguay.
The motion of the Hon. Member for Portage-Marquette (Mr. Mayer) is true in what it says. It condemns the Government "for its failure to recognize the economic hardship affecting all farmers in Canada". It has never been a more true statement than it is today. The Hon. Member for Cari-boo-Chilcotin (Mr. Greenaway) gave one very clear example of it in his speech. Another example of the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) not recognizing the difficulty in the vegetable and potato industry was put before the House by the Hon. Member for Carleton-Charlotte (Mr. McCain). Also, the Hon. Member for Assiniboia (Mr. Gustafson) put in very clear language the difficulties with the agricultural grain stabilization plan at a time when grain farmers in western Canada have been severely hurt by difficult economic times. Almost $1 billion of their own money is sitting in the federal Treasury, and the Government is not prepared to change the formula so that the money can get to those farmers in need at this time, not a year or two years from now.
These examples were put before the House. The Hon. Member for Portage-Marquette dealt with a group of plans which have been put in place for agriculture over the last 40 years. If we look at the record of the Minister and the number of Bills he has put before the House in the last ten years, we find that most of them were only improvements on legislation passed before he ever became Minister. The Hon. Member for Portage-Marquette suggested that the Minister should use the tools which are in place at this time if he has no new ideas to put before the House to assist farmers in difficult times.
If we look at the net incomes of farmers, as the Hon. Member for Humboldt-Lake Centre (Mr. Althouse) pointed out, we see that in net constant dollars farmers in 1982 were making less than they were making in 1956. That is very
Supply
eye-opening because there are fewer farmers today than there were at that time. If we look at farm expenses, we find that they have increased tremendously. It makes me wonder how they are capable of hanging on, given that statistical picture. Farm production costs are estimated to increase from 1981 to 1986 by 110 per cent. If we look at the prices of commodities, we find that there is no chance for that kind of increase in commodity prices to keep up with expenses.
Basically, the motion is saying that we need some policies to bring agriculture into the eighties and to carry it into the nineties. The Minister should not sit back and brag about the policies on which he has sat during the ten years he has been Minister of Agriculture. They are not sufficient to carry us into the next decade. That is why the motion condemns the Government for its failure to implement sound agricultural policies to carry us into these coming years. This is very evident to farmers throughout the country.
I know time is drawing to an end, but in conclusion I ask the Government to look at the agricultural adjustment fund to deal with western livestock affected in the Crow debate. It is most important if it intends to continue on the path in the Crow debate which it has followed to this point.
